What is meant by this is that, following the obligation upon them of pilgrimage to Bayt al-Maqdis, they were commanded that when they performed the pilgrimage they should bring with them the firstborn of their flocks and the firstborn of the produce of their land. This is because it had been obligatory upon them before that the young of the sheep and cattle be left with their mothers for seven days, and from the eighth day onward it became fit to be an offering. So by this text, with His words "you shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk," He pointed to the fact that they should not be excessive in prolonging the stay of the firstborn young of cattle and sheep with their mothers. Rather, when they went on pilgrimage to Bayt al-Maqdis, they would bring with them their firstborn, which had passed seven days since birth, to take them as offerings.

But the foolish shaykhs imagined that the Law meant "boiling" as cooking in a pot, and that they had been forbidden to cook kid meat in milk.

This error in interpreting this word was not enough for them. They forbade eating all kinds of meat with milk, thereby disregarding the word "kid," disregarding the word "its mother," and imposing upon the text what it cannot bear. When they wanted to eat meat and milk, they ate each of them separately. The matter in this and similar cases is minor.

(Section)

It is not strange that this entire nation agrees upon the impossible and unites upon kinds of error.

When a state dies out from a nation through the conquest of others over it and their seizing it, the landmarks of its religion are obliterated and its traces are effaced.

The loss of a state comes about through successive raids and battles, and the destruction and burning of lands. These matters continue to recur upon it until its knowledge turns into ignorance, its might into humiliation, and its abundance into scarcity.

Whenever a nation is more ancient, and the states that subjugate it with humiliation and disgrace have succeeded one another over it, its share of the obliteration of its religion's landmarks and traces is greater.

This nation has the greatest share of this matter, because it is among the most ancient nations, and because of the many nations that have conquered it: the Chaldeans, the Babylonians, the Persians, the Greeks, the Christians, and finally the Muslims.

Of these nations, none sought their extermination, went to excess in burning their lands and books, and cut off their traces, except the Muslims. They were the most just of the nations toward them and toward others, in observance of God's command concerning them, where He said:

﴿O you who believe, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more deserving of both. So do not follow your desires, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allah is ever, with what you do, Acquainted﴾ [An-Nisa: 135], and He says: ﴿O you who believe, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 8].

Islam encountered this nation under the protection of the Persians and the protection of the Christians, such that they no longer had a city or an army.

The most honoured of this nation whom Islam encountered were the Jews of Khaybar and Madinah and what was around them.

They had only headed to that region because of what they had been promised about the appearance of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family). They used to fight the polytheists of the Arabs, and they would seek victory over them by believing in the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family) before his appearance, and they would promise them that a prophet would come whom they would follow, and with whom they would kill them with the killing of 'Ad and Iram.

When Allah, mighty and majestic, sent His Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family), those Arabs whom they used to fight had already preceded them to him. Envy and transgression then led them to disbelieve in him and to deny him.

What was most grievous to this wrathful nation of that was what befell them at the hands of the rebellious kings and other kings of the Israelites, who killed the prophets and went to great lengths in pursuing them, who worshipped idols, who brought from the lands their custodians to learn the rites of worship, who built temples and sanctuaries for them, who devoted themselves to their worship, and who abandoned the rulings of the Torah for successive ages.

If this was the constant succession of calamities upon their religion from their own kings and from themselves, then what is to be thought of the calamities that befell them from other than their kings, and the killing of their leaders, and the burning of their books, and the prevention of them from practising their religion?

The Persians often prevented them from circumcision, and often prevented them from prayer, knowing that the greater part of this group's prayer was supplication against nations for destruction, and against the world for ruin, apart from their own lands, which is the land of Canaan.

When this nation saw the Persians' severity in preventing them from prayer, they invented supplications which they claimed were sections of their prayer, which they called the Hazzana (the chanting of a cantor, a liturgical recitation set to melody). They composed numerous melodies for them, and they would gather at their prayer times to chant and recite them. They called the one who performed them the Hazzan (cantor).

The difference between this and prayer is that prayer is without melody, and the worshipper recites the prayer alone, and no one else raises his voice with him. The Hazzan is joined by others in raising their voices in the Hazzana, and they assist him in the melodies.

So when the Persians objected to them doing that, the Jews said: "We are sometimes lamenting and mourning over ourselves," and they would leave them alone.

When Islam came and confirmed them in their prayer, they retained that Hazzana and did not abandon it.

These are brief sections on the plotting of Satan and his manipulation of this nation, by which the upright Muslim may come to know the measure of Allah's blessing upon him, and the favour of knowledge and faith with which He has graced him, and by which whoever among the seekers of truth from this nation whom Allah, exalted is He, wills to guide may be guided.

From Allah comes success and guidance to the straight path. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

(Section)

Among these is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So We stirred up among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾

And His saying: ﴿And We cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾

This stirring up and casting is purely His action, and the mutual enmity and hatred are its effect, which is purely their action. The root of the misguidance of the Qadariyyah and the Jabriyyah lies in their failure to be guided to the distinction between His action and the action of the servant. The Jabriyyah made mutual enmity and hatred the action of the Lord alone, without the two who are at enmity and hatred. The Qadariyyah made it purely their own action, in which God has no creation, no power, and no will. The people of the upright path made it their action, and it is an effect of God's action, power and will, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea﴾

So the enabling is His action, and the traveling is the action of the servants, and it is the effect of His enabling. Likewise, guidance and misguidance are His action, while being guided and being misguided are the effect of His action, and they are our actions that subsist in us. So He is the Guide and the servant is the one who is guided, and He is the one who misguides whom He wills, and the servant is the one who is misguided. This is the truth, and this is the truth, and both groups have deviated from the straight path.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 5, verse 18:

His statement in Surat al-Ma'ida, in refutation of their claim, "We are the children of God and His beloved. Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins?" means that a father does not punish his son, and a beloved does not punish his beloved.

Here there is a very subtle point, which few notice. We establish it by means of a question and an answer.

If it is said: it is known that a father may discipline his child when he misbehaves, and a beloved may shun his beloved when he sees in him something he dislikes?

It is answered: If you reflect, O questioner, on His words, "Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins?", you will know the difference between this punishment and shunning and discipline. Punishment for sin is the fruit of anger, which is incompatible with love. So if love were present, as they claimed, there would be no sins for which they deserve punishment: transformation into apes and swine, the domination of their enemies who plunder them, enslave them, destroy their places of worship, and take their offspring captive.

A lover does not do this to his beloved, nor does a father do it to his son.

It is well known that the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, does not do this to a nation except after its extreme criminality, its rebellion against God, and its arrogance in refusing His obedience and worship. That contradicts their being His beloved. Had they loved Him, they would not have committed the acts of His anger and wrath that brought this upon them. And had He loved them, He would have disciplined them and not punished them.

So discipline is one thing, and punishment is another.

Discipline is intended for refinement, mercy and correction, whereas punishment is for retribution and recompense for vile deeds. This is one kind, and that is another.

(Benefit)

If there were nothing in the love of God except that it saves its lover from His punishment, the servant should never accept anything in exchange for it.

Some scholars were asked: Where do you find in the Qur'an that a beloved does not punish his beloved? He answered with His words, may He be exalted, "The Jews and the Christians said: We are the children of God and His beloved. Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins?" and the rest of the verse.

Imam Ahmad said: Isma'il ibn Yunus narrated to us from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, Allah does not punish His beloved, but He may test him in this world."

Imam Ahmad said: Sayyar narrated to us, Ja'far narrated to us, Abu Ghalib narrated to us, saying: We have been told that this statement is from the counsel of Jesus son of Mary: "O assembly of the disciples, make yourselves beloved to God by hating the people of sin, draw near to Him by detesting them, and seek His pleasure by their displeasure." They said: "O Prophet of God, whom then should we sit with?" He said: "Sit with those whose speech increases your deeds, whose sight reminds you of God, and whose knowledge makes you disinterested in your worldly life."

Sufficient as an immediate reward for turning to God, may He be exalted, is that God turns the hearts of His servants toward whoever turns to Him, just as He turns their hearts away from whoever turns away from Him. The hearts of the servants are in God's hand, not in their own hands.

Imam Ahmad said: Hasan, in the transmission of Shayban, narrated to us from Qatada, who said: We were told that Hirm ibn Hayyan used to say: "No servant turns to God with his heart except that Almighty God turns the hearts of the believers toward him, until He grants him their affection and mercy."

This has also been related as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report, with the wording: "No servant turns to God with his heart except that Almighty God turns toward him the hearts of His servants, makes their hearts hasten to him with love and mercy, and God is quicker to every good toward him." Since hearts are created inclined to love the one who does good to them, and every blessing that reaches the servant is from God, as God, the Exalted, said: "And whatever blessing you have is from God" (16:53), then none is more base than one who occupies his heart with love of other than Him.

Imam Ahmad said: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, saying: al-A'mash narrated to me from al-Minhal, from Abdullah ibn al-Harith, who said: God revealed to Dawud, peace be upon him: "O Dawud, love Me and make My servants love Me, and make Me beloved to My servants." He said: "O Lord, I love You; how shall I make You beloved to Your servants?" He said: "Remind them of Me, for they mention of Me only what is good."

Among the most excellent things one may ask of God, may He be exalted, is His love, the love of those who love Him, and the love of deeds that bring one closer to His love. Among the most comprehensive supplications for this is to say: "O God, I ask You for Your love, the love of those who love You, and the love of deeds that bring me closer to Your love. O God, whatever You grant me of what I love, make it a strength for me in what You love, and whatever You withhold from me of what I love, make it a leisure for me in what You love. O God, make Your love dearer to me than my family, my wealth, and cold water on thirst. O God, make me beloved to You, to Your angels, Your prophets, Your messengers and Your righteous servants, and make me among those who love You and love Your angels, Your prophets, Your messengers and Your righteous servants. O God, give life to my heart with Your love, and make me for You as You love. O God, make me love You with my whole heart and please You with all my effort. O God, make all my love for You and all my striving in seeking Your pleasure."

This supplication is the central pillar of the tent of Islam, upon which its structure rests, and it is the reality of the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Those who truly uphold this reality are those by whose testimony the faith stands. God, glorified is He, made Himself known to His servants through His names, attributes and actions in a way that necessitates their love for Him, for hearts are instinctively disposed to love perfection and whoever possesses it. God, glorified and exalted is He, possesses absolute perfection from every aspect, with no deficiency in any respect. He is the Beautiful, than whom none is more beautiful. Indeed, even if the beauty of all creation were upon one man among them, and they all possessed that beauty, their beauty would have no comparison at all to the beauty of God; the comparison would be less than that of a weak lamp to the sphere of the sun. "To God belongs the highest likeness" (16:60).

It has also been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed God is Beautiful and loves beauty."

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 5, verses 21–22:

Indeed, Allah, glorified is He, rescued them from Pharaoh, his authority and his oppression, parted the sea for them, showed them the signs and wonders, granted them victory, sheltered them and honoured them, and gave them what He had given to no one among the worlds.

Then He commanded them to enter the land which Allah had prescribed for them. Included in this was a glad tidings to them that they would be victorious and that it would be opened to them, and that this land was theirs. But they refused to obey Him and to comply with His command, and they met this command and this glad tidings with their words: ﴿Go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]

And reflect: the Prophet of Allah, Musa (peace be upon him), was gentle with them, good in his address to them, reminding them of the blessings of Allah upon them, giving them the glad tidings of Allah's promise that the land was written for them, and warning them against disobeying Him by turning back on their heels, and that if they disobeyed His command and did not comply, they would become losers.

So he combined for them the command and the prohibition, the glad tidings and the warning, the encouragement and the intimidation, and the reminder of past blessings. Yet they met him with the worst of responses. They opposed the command of Allah with their words: ﴿O Musa, indeed there are in it a people of tyrants.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22]

So they did not show reverence to the Messenger of Allah and His interlocutor, to the extent that they called him by his name and did not say, "O Prophet of Allah." They said, "Indeed, there are in it a people of tyrants," and forgot the power of the Tyrant of the heavens and the earth, who humbles the tyrants to those who obey Him. Their fear of those tyrants, whose foreheads are in the hand of Allah, was greater than their fear of the Most High Tyrant, glorified is He, and their dread of those tyrants in their hearts was stronger than their dread of Him.

Then they openly declared disobedience and refusal to obey. They said: ﴿Indeed, we will never enter it as long as they are in it.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22]

They emphasised their disobedience with several kinds of emphasis.

The first: they prepared an excuse for their disobedience by saying: ﴿Indeed, there are in it a people of tyrants.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22]

The second: their explicit declaration that they would not obey. They opened the sentence with the emphatic particle "inna" and then confirmed the negation with the particle "lan," which denotes negation of the future: that is, we will not enter it now, nor in the future.

Then they made their entry conditional upon the tyrants leaving it. So a man said to them: ﴿Two men from those who fear [Allah], upon whom Allah had bestowed His favour.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23]

[They were] those who fear Allah, through their obedience and submission to His command. This is the view of the majority, and it is the correct one. It was said: those who fear the tyrants, who embraced Islam and followed Musa (peace be upon him). ﴿Enter upon them through the gate.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23]

That is, the gate of the city. Charge upon them, for they have been filled with terror of you. ﴿For when you enter it, indeed you will be the victors.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23]

Then he guided them to what would secure victory and triumph for them, which is reliance upon Allah.

The people's answer was: ﴿They said, "O Musa, indeed we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]

Glorified is He whose forbearance is great, that He is met with such a response to His command, and His messenger is addressed with such words, and He is patient with them, does not hasten to punish them, but His forbearance and generosity encompassed them. The most severe punishment He inflicted upon them was that He made them wander in the wilderness of the Tih for forty years, the cloud shading them from the heat, and manna and quails being sent down upon them.

In the two Sahihs, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I witnessed from al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad a stance that would be dearer to me than anything else I could be equal to. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was supplicating against the polytheists, and said: 'We will not say to you what the people of Musa said to Musa: Go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting right here. Rather, we will fight on your right and on your left, before you and behind you.' I saw the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brighten at that and he was delighted by it."

They did not meet the Prophet of Allah with this kind of response.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 5, verses 21–22:

Indeed, Allah, glorified is He, rescued them from Pharaoh, his authority and his oppression, parted the sea for them, showed them the signs and wonders, granted them victory, sheltered them and honoured them, and gave them what He had given to no one among the worlds.

Then He commanded them to enter the land which Allah had prescribed for them. Included in this was a glad tidings to them that they would be victorious and that it would be opened to them, and that this land was theirs. But they refused to obey Him and to comply with His command, and they met this command and this glad tidings with their words: ﴿Go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]

And reflect: the Prophet of Allah, Musa (peace be upon him), was gentle with them, good in his address to them, reminding them of the blessings of Allah upon them, giving them the glad tidings of Allah's promise that the land was written for them, and warning them against disobeying Him by turning back on their heels, and that if they disobeyed His command and did not comply, they would become losers.

So he combined for them the command and the prohibition, the glad tidings and the warning, the encouragement and the intimidation, and the reminder of past blessings. Yet they met him with the worst of responses. They opposed the command of Allah with their words: ﴿O Musa, indeed there are in it a people of tyrants.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22]

So they did not show reverence to the Messenger of Allah and His interlocutor, to the extent that they called him by his name and did not say, "O Prophet of Allah." They said, "Indeed, there are in it a people of tyrants," and forgot the power of the Tyrant of the heavens and the earth, who humbles the tyrants to those who obey Him. Their fear of those tyrants, whose foreheads are in the hand of Allah, was greater than their fear of the Most High Tyrant, glorified is He, and their dread of those tyrants in their hearts was stronger than their dread of Him.

Then they openly declared disobedience and refusal to obey. They said: ﴿Indeed, we will never enter it as long as they are in it.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22]

They emphasised their disobedience with several kinds of emphasis.

The first: they prepared an excuse for their disobedience by saying: ﴿Indeed, there are in it a people of tyrants.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22]

The second: their explicit declaration that they would not obey. They opened the sentence with the emphatic particle "inna" and then confirmed the negation with the particle "lan," which denotes negation of the future: that is, we will not enter it now, nor in the future.

Then they made their entry conditional upon the tyrants leaving it. So a man said to them: ﴿Two men from those who fear [Allah], upon whom Allah had bestowed His favour.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23]

[They were] those who fear Allah, through their obedience and submission to His command. This is the view of the majority, and it is the correct one. It was said: those who fear the tyrants, who embraced Islam and followed Musa (peace be upon him). ﴿Enter upon them through the gate.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23]

That is, the gate of the city. Charge upon them, for they have been filled with terror of you. ﴿For when you enter it, indeed you will be the victors.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23]

Then he guided them to what would secure victory and triumph for them, which is reliance upon Allah.

The people's answer was: ﴿They said, "O Musa, indeed we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]

Glorified is He whose forbearance is great, that He is met with such a response to His command, and His messenger is addressed with such words, and He is patient with them, does not hasten to punish them, but His forbearance and generosity encompassed them. The most severe punishment He inflicted upon them was that He made them wander in the wilderness of the Tih for forty years, the cloud shading them from the heat, and manna and quails being sent down upon them.

In the two Sahihs, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I witnessed from al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad a stance that would be dearer to me than anything else I could be equal to. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was supplicating against the polytheists, and said: 'We will not say to you what the people of Musa said to Musa: Go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting right here. Rather, we will fight on your right and on your left, before you and behind you.' I saw the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brighten at that and he was delighted by it."

They did not meet the Prophet of Allah with this kind of response.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 5, verse 23 (part 1 of 4):

Among the stations (manazil) of ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ is the station of tawakkul (trust in God).

God Most High says: ﴿And upon God rely, if you are believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23]. He says: ﴿And let the believers rely upon God﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 122]. He says: ﴿And whoever relies upon God, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]. He speaks of His friends (awliya'): ﴿Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have turned, and to You is the final return﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. He says to His Messenger: ﴿Say, "He is the Most Merciful; we have believed in Him, and upon Him we have relied"﴾ [al-Mulk: 29]. He says to His Messenger ﷺ: ﴿So rely upon God; indeed, you are upon the clear truth﴾ [al-Naml: 79]. He says to him: ﴿And rely upon God, and sufficient is God as a Guardian﴾ [al-Nisa': 81]. He says to him: ﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die, and glorify Him with His praise﴾ [al-Furqan: 58]. He says to him: ﴿And when you have determined, then rely upon God; indeed, God loves those who rely upon Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 159]. He speaks of His prophets and messengers: ﴿And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us to our ways?﴾ [Ibrahim: 12]. He speaks of the companions of His Prophet: ﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them," but it increased them in faith, and they said, "Sufficient for us is God, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 173]. And He says: ﴿The believers are only those who, when God is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely﴾ [al-Anfal: 2].

The Qur'an is full of this.

In the two Sahihs, in the hadith of the seventy thousand who will enter Paradise without reckoning: "They are those who do not seek incantation (istirqa'), nor do they believe in omens (tatayyur), nor do they seek cauterization (ikhtiwa'), and upon their Lord they rely."

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "Sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said it when he was thrown into the fire, and Muhammad (ﷺ) said it when they said to him: ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them, but it increased them in faith, and they said, "Sufficient for us is God, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 173].

In the two Sahihs, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "O Allah, to You I have submitted, in You I have believed, upon You I have relied, to You I have turned in repentance, and by You I contend. O Allah, I seek refuge in Your might, there is no god but You, that You should lead me astray. You are the Ever-Living who does not die, while the jinn and mankind die."

In al-Tirmidhi, from 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you truly relied upon Allah with the reliance due to Him, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out hungry in the morning and return full in the evening."

In the Sunan, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says, when he leaves his house, 'In the name of Allah, I have relied upon Allah, and there is no power and no strength except by Allah,' it is said to him: 'You have been guided, protected, and sufficed.' Then the devil says to another devil: 'How can you deal with a man who has been guided, sufficed, and protected?'"

Tawakkul is half of the religion, and the other half is inabah (turning to Allah), for religion is seeking help (isti'anah) and worship ('ibadah).

So tawakkul is the seeking of help, and inabah is the worship.

Its station is the broadest and most comprehensive of the stations, and it is never without its inhabitants, due to the breadth of what tawakkul relates to, the multitude of the needs of all beings, and the generality of tawakkul and its occurrence among believers and disbelievers, the righteous and the wicked, and birds, beasts, and animals. The inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, the accountable and others, are in the station of tawakkul, though the objects of their tawakkul differ. His friends and intimates rely upon Him in faith, in supporting His religion, in raising His word, in struggling against His enemies, in what He loves, and in carrying out His commands.

Below these are those who rely upon Him in their own steadfastness and in keeping their state with Allah, free from concern for people.

Below these are those who rely upon Him for a known benefit they obtain from Him, such as provision, health, victory over an enemy, a wife or child, and the like.

Below these are those who rely upon Him for the attainment of sin and immoral acts. The people of these aims generally obtain them only by seeking help from Allah and relying upon Him; indeed, their tawakkul may be stronger than the tawakkul of many people of acts of obedience. For this reason they throw themselves into destruction and ruin, depending upon Allah to save them and grant them their aims.

The best tawakkul is tawakkul in what is obligatory: I mean the obligation of the Truth (God), the obligation toward creation, and the obligation toward the self. The broadest and most beneficial of it is tawakkul in effecting a result in the external world for a religious benefit, or in averting a religious harm. This is the tawakkul of the prophets in establishing the religion of Allah and repelling the corruption of corrupters on earth, and this is the tawakkul of their heirs. Then people differ in tawakkul according to their aspirations and purposes: one relies upon Allah in attaining kingship, another in attaining a loaf of bread.

Whoever sincerely relies upon Allah for attaining something he obtains: if it is beloved and pleasing to Him, he has the praiseworthy outcome; if it is hated and displeasing to Him, what he obtains through his tawakkul is a harm to him; and if it is permissible, he obtains the benefit of tawakkul without the benefit of what he relied upon, if he does not seek help through it in his acts of obedience. And Allah knows best.

[Section: The meaning of tawakkul]

Section

Let us mention the meaning of tawakkul, its degrees, and what has been said about it.

Imam Ahmad said: "Tawakkul is an action of the heart." That is, it is an action of the heart, not a statement of the tongue, nor an action of the limbs, nor is it of the category of knowledge and perceptions.

Among the people are those who place it in the category of knowledge and cognitions, and say: it is the heart's knowledge of the Lord's sufficiency for the servant.

Among them are those who interpret it as stillness and the cessation of the heart's motion, and say: tawakkul is the heart's casting itself before the Lord, like the casting of a corpse before the washer, with his heart as he wills. It is leaving off choice and yielding to the courses of decrees.

Sahl said: "Tawakkul is yielding to Allah with whatever He wills."

Among them are those who interpret it as contentment, and say: it is contentment with what is decreed.

Bishr al-Hafi said: "One of them says, 'I have relied upon Allah,' and lies against Allah. If he had truly relied upon Allah, he would be content with what Allah does."

Yahya ibn Mu'adh was asked: "When is a man a mutawakkil?" He said: "When he is content with Allah as Disposer."

Among them are those who interpret it as trust in Allah, reassurance in Him, and tranquility toward Him.

Ibn 'Ata' said: "Tawakkul is that no restlessness toward means appears in you, despite your intense need for them, and that you do not depart from the reality of tranquility toward the Truth while being aware of them."

Dhu al-Nun said: "It is leaving off the management of the self and divesting oneself of power and strength. The servant is only able to rely upon Allah when he knows that the Truth, glorified is He, knows and sees what he is in."

Some of them said: "Tawakkul is attachment to Allah in every state."

It was said: "Tawakkul is that the lacks of need come upon you, and you aspire only to Him in whom all sufficiency lies."

It was said: "It is the negation of doubts and the entrusting of affairs to the Owner of kings."

Dhu al-Nun said: "It is the removal of lords and the cutting of means." He means cutting them off from the attachment of the heart to them, not from the limbs' engagement with them.

Among them are those who made it composed of two or more matters.

Abu Sa'id al-Kharraz said: "Tawakkul is agitation without stillness, and stillness without agitation."

He means: the movement of one's self among means outwardly and inwardly, with stillness toward the Causer and reliance upon Him; his heart is not agitated with Him, and his movement is not stilled from the means that lead to His pleasure.

Abu Turab al-Nakhshabi said: "It is casting the body into servitude ('ubudiyyah), the heart's attachment to Lordship (rububiyyah), and tranquility in the sufficiency [of God]. If he is given, he gives thanks; if he is denied, he is patient."

So he made it composed of five matters: standing up to the movements of servitude, the heart's attachment to the Lord's management, its stillness toward His decree and destiny, its tranquility and His sufficiency for it, its gratitude when He gives, and its patience when He withholds.

Abu Ya'qub al-Nahrajuri said: "Tawakkul upon Allah is with the perfection of reality (haqiqiyyah), as occurred to Ibrahim the Friend (peace be upon him) at the time he said to Jibril (peace be upon him): 'As for you, no.' For he was absent from himself through Allah, and so he did not see with Allah other than Allah."

The people agreed that tawakkul does not contradict standing by the means. Tawakkul is not valid except with the standing by them; otherwise it is idleness and corrupt tawakkul.

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: "Whoever finds fault with movement has found fault with the Sunnah, and whoever finds fault with tawakkul has found fault with faith."

So tawakkul is the state of the Prophet (ﷺ), and earning (kasb) is his Sunnah. Whoever acts according to his state, let him not abandon his Sunnah. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Sa'id: "It is agitation without stillness, and stillness without agitation," and Sahl's saying is clearer and more elevated.

It was said: "Tawakkul is cutting the heart's ties to other than Allah."

Sahl was asked about tawakkul, and he said: "A heart that lived with Allah without an attachment."

It was said: "Tawakkul is abandoning attachments and being continually joined to the realities."

It was said: "Tawakkul is that abundance and scarcity are equal to you."

This is among its requirements and effects, not its essence.

It was said: "It is leaving every means that connects you to the Causer, until the Truth alone is the one who takes charge of that."

This is correct in one respect and false in another. Leaving the commanded means is detrimental to tawakkul, and Allah has undertaken to connect the servant through them. As for leaving permissible means: if leaving them is for something more beneficial than them, it is praiseworthy; otherwise it is blameworthy.

It was said: "It is casting the self into servitude and removing it from lordship."

He means its surrender to the command, its innocence from its own power and strength, and witnessing that through it, but rather through the Lord alone.

Some said: "Tawakkul is submission to the command and decree of the Lord."

Some said: "It is entrusting oneself to Him in every state."

Some made tawakkul a beginning, submission an intermediate, and entrusting a final end.

Abu 'Ali al-Daqqaq said: "Tawakkul has three degrees: tawakkul, then taslim (submission), then tafwid (entrusting). The one who relies (mutawakkil) is at rest in His promise; the one of submission (taslim) is content with His knowledge; the one of entrusting (tafwid) is pleased with His judgment. So tawakkul is a beginning, taslim is an intermediate, and tafwid is an end. Tawakkul is the attribute of the believers, taslim is the attribute of the friends (awliya'), and tafwid is the attribute of the monotheists (muwahhidun).

Tawakkul is the attribute of the common folk, taslim is the attribute of the elite (khawass), and tafwid is the attribute of the elite of the elite.

Tawakkul is the attribute of the prophets, taslim is the attribute of Ibrahim the Friend, and tafwid is the attribute of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and upon them all be peace."

This is all the words of al-Daqqaq. The meaning of this tawakkul is reliance upon the Trustee (wakil), and a man may rely upon his agent while still having some kind of demand upon him, will, and a trace of contention. When he yields to him, that leaves him, and he is content with what his agent does. The state of the one who entrusts is above this, for he is a seeker and a desirer from the one to whom he entrusts, asking him to take charge of his affairs. So it is contentment and choice, and submission and reliance. Tawakkul is included in taslim, and both are included in tafwid. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

[The reality of tawakkul is composed of matters]

[Section: The first: knowledge of the Lord and His attributes]

Section

The reality of the matter is that tawakkul is a state composed of a collection of matters, and the reality of tawakkul is not complete except with them. Each one pointed to one of these matters, or two, or more.

The first of these is knowledge of the Lord and His attributes: His power, His sufficiency, His self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah), the ending of affairs in His knowledge, and their issuing from His will and power. This knowledge is the first degree by which the servant places his foot in the station of tawakkul.

Our Shaykh, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "For this reason tawakkul is not valid and cannot be conceived from a philosopher, nor from the Qadariyyah deniers who say that in His dominion there is what He does not will, nor does it stand from the Jahmiyyah deniers of the attributes of the Lord, majestic is His majesty. Tawakkul stands only from the people of affirmation (ithbat)."

The Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 5, Verse 23 (Part 2 of 4)

Then what trust (tawakkul, reliance upon God) can there be for one who believes that Allah does not encompass the particulars of the world, both its lowest and highest parts? Nor that He acts by His own choice? Nor that He has will and volition? Nor that He has attributes subsisting in Him? Whoever knows Allah and His attributes better and more thoroughly, his trust is sounder and stronger. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

[Section: The Second Level: Affirming Causes and Their Effects]

The second level: affirming causes (asbab) and their effects (musabbabat).

Whoever denies them, his trust is flawed. This is the reverse of what appears to shallow opinion, which holds that affirming causes detracts from trust, and that negating them is the perfection of trust.

Know that those who deny causes cannot have true trust at all, because trust is among the strongest causes for attaining what one trusts in. It is like supplication (du'a'), which Allah made a cause for obtaining what is asked for. If the servant believes that his trust was not appointed by Allah as a cause, nor that his supplication was made a cause for attaining anything, then whatever he trusts in and asks for will, if it has been decreed, come to pass whether he trusts or not, supplicates or not; and if it has not been decreed, it will not come to pass, whether he trusts or abandons trust.

These people declare that trust and supplication are pure servitude ('ubudiyya mahda), with no benefit other than that. And if the servant abandons trust and supplication, nothing that was decreed for him would be lost. Among their extremists are those who consider the supplication for forgiveness of error and forgetfulness to be useless, since its outcome is guaranteed.

I have seen one of the more profound of these people, in one of his books, forbidding this supplication, permitting it only as recitation and not as supplication. He said: because supplicating with it implies doubt about its occurrence, since the supplicant is between fear and hope, and doubt about its occurrence is doubt about the report of Allah. Look at the monstrous consequences that denying causes has led to, and the prohibition of supplicating with what Allah praised His servants and friends for asking. The Muslims, from the time of their Prophet (ﷺ) until now, have continued to supplicate with it in moments of supplication, and it is among the most excellent supplications.

The answer to this false illusion is: there remains a third category, other than the two you mentioned, which you have not mentioned, and which is the reality. It is that Allah has decreed the occurrence of a thing upon the occurrence of its cause, such as trust and supplication. He has therefore appointed supplication and trust as two causes for the attainment of the sought-after object. Allah decreed that it would occur when the servant performs its cause; so when he does not bring about the cause, the effect is impossible.

This is like how He decreed the birth of a child when a man has intercourse with a woman; if he does not have intercourse, the child is not created. He decreed satiety when one eats, and quenching of thirst when one drinks; if one does not do so, one will not be satiated nor quenched. He decreed the completion of the pilgrimage and arrival at Makkah when one travels and takes the road; if one sits in his house, he will not reach Makkah. He decreed entry into Paradise for one who embraces Islam and performs righteous deeds; if he abandons Islam and does not do righteous deeds, he will never enter it. He decreed the cooking of food by lighting fire beneath it. And He decreed the sprouting of grains that are sown by tilling the earth and casting seed into it; whoever does not do this gets nothing but disappointment.

The parallel to what the deniers of causes say is that each of these people abandons the connecting cause and says: if it was decreed for me, and it was written in eternity, that I would have a child, be satiated, be quenched, or perform the pilgrimage and the like, then it will reach me, whether I move or stay still, marry or refrain, travel or sit. And if it was not decreed for me, it will not come to me either, whether I act or refrain.

Does anyone count this among the intelligent? Are not beasts more discerning than such a person? For the beast strives for the cause through general guidance.

Trust is among the greatest causes through which the sought-after object is attained and the disliked thing is averted. Whoever denies causes, his trust cannot be upright. However, part of the perfection of trust is not to rely upon causes, and to sever the heart's attachment to them, so that the state of his heart is standing with Allah, not with the causes, while the state of his body is standing with the causes.

Causes are the locus of Allah's wisdom, His command, and His religion. Trust is connected to His lordship, His decree, and His destiny. The servitude of causes stands only on the leg of trust, and the leg of trust stands only on the foot of servitude. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

[Section: The Third Level: The Heart's Firm Establishment in the Station of the Oneness of Trust]

The third level: the heart's firm establishment in the station of the oneness (tawhid) of trust.

The servant's trust will not be upright until his tawhid is sound. Indeed, the reality of trust is the oneness of the heart. As long as the attachments of shirk remain in it, his trust is defective and flawed. The soundness of trust is in proportion to the purity of tawhid, for whenever the servant turns toward other than Allah, that turning takes a branch of his heart. His trust in Allah decreases in proportion to the loss of that branch. From here, some have thought that trust cannot be sound except by abandoning causes. This is true, but the abandonment is of causes in the heart, not in the limbs. Trust is not complete except by abandoning causes in the heart while the limbs are attached to them. So he is detached from them inwardly and connected to them outwardly. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

[Section: The Fourth Level: The Heart's Reliance upon Allah, Its Leaning upon Him, and Its Tranquility in Him]

The fourth level: the heart's reliance upon Allah, its leaning upon Him, and its tranquility in Him.

So that no agitation remains in it from the disturbance of causes, nor any tranquility in them; rather, it strips the tranquility in them from its heart and clothes itself in tranquility in their Causer.

The sign of this is that he is not concerned about their coming or going. His heart does not become agitated or tremble when what he loves of them departs or what he dislikes approaches, because his reliance upon Allah, his tranquility in Him, and his leaning upon Him have protected him from both fear and hope of them. His state is like that of one against whom a great enemy has come out, against whom he has no power; he sees an open fortress, and his Lord has led him into it and closed its gate behind him. He sees his enemy outside the fortress. The agitation of his heart and his fear of the enemy in this state have no meaning.

Likewise, a man to whom a king gave a dirham, which was then stolen from him. The king says to him: I have many times that amount; do not worry. Whenever you come to me, I will give you many times that from my treasuries. When he knows the truth of the king's word, trusts him, is at peace with him, and knows that his treasuries are full of such things, the loss does not grieve him.

This has been illustrated by the state of the nursing infant in its reliance and tranquility, at peace with his mother's breast, knowing nothing else. There is no attention in his heart to anything else. As one of the knowers (arifun) said: the one who trusts is like the infant, who knows nothing to take refuge in except his mother's breast. Likewise, the one who trusts takes refuge only in his Lord, glorified is He.

[Section: The Fifth Level: Good Opinion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic]

The fifth level: good opinion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

In proportion to the goodness of your opinion of your Lord and your hope in Him, your trust in Him will be. For this reason, some have defined trust as good opinion of Allah.

The verification is that good opinion of Him calls one to trust in Him, since trust cannot be conceived in one whose opinion of Him is bad, nor in one whom you do not hope in. And Allah knows best.

[Section: The Sixth Level: The Heart's Surrender to Allah]

The sixth level: the heart's surrender to Him, the drawing of all its motives toward Him, and the cutting off of its disputes.

It was explained in this way by one who said: that the servant should be before Allah like the corpse before the one washing it, who turns it however he wishes, with no movement or planning from it. This is the meaning of the saying of some of them: trust is the abandonment of planning, meaning surrender to the Lord's planning for you. This applies outside the domain of command and prohibition, rather in what He does to you, not in what He commands you to do.

Surrender is like the humble slave's submission of himself to his master, his yielding to him, and his abandonment of the disputes of his own self and its will against his master. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

[Section: The Seventh Level: Tafwid (Entrusting)]

The seventh level: tafwid (entrusting).

It is the spirit, core, and reality of trust. It is the casting of all one's affairs upon Allah and the placing of them with Him, by choice and seeking, not by compulsion and necessity. It is like the entrusting of a weak, helpless, overpowered son of his affairs to his father, all of them, knowing his father's compassion for him, his mercy, his complete sufficiency, the goodness of his guardianship over him, and his management of his affairs. He sees that his father's management of him is better than his own management of himself, and that his father's care for his interests and his assumption of them is better than his own care for his own interests and his assumption of them. He finds nothing more beneficial or gentle for himself than entrusting all his affairs to his father, and his rest from bearing their burdens and the weight of their load, along with his own incapacity to handle them, his ignorance of the aspects of their benefit, and his knowledge of the perfect knowledge, power, and compassion of the one to whom he has entrusted them.

[Section: The Fruit of Trust]

When he places his foot upon this level, he moves from it to the level of contentment (rida').

This is the fruit of trust. Whoever defines trust by it has defined it by its most sublime fruit and greatest benefit, for when one truly trusts, he is content with what his trustee does.

Our shaykh (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say: the decreed matter is surrounded by two things: trust before it, and contentment after it. Whoever trusts in Allah before the action, and is content with what is decreed for him after the action, has fulfilled servitude, or words to this effect.

I say: this is the meaning of the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the supplication of istikhara (seeking guidance): "O Allah, I seek Your guidance by Your knowledge, and I seek power by Your power, and I ask You of Your great bounty." This is trust and entrusting. Then he said: "For You know and I do not know, You are capable and I am not capable, and You are the Knower of the unseen." This is disavowal before Allah of knowledge, strength, and power, and seeking nearness to Him, glorified is He, through His attributes, which are the dearest means by which those who seek nearness can draw close to Him. Then he asked his Lord to decree that matter for him if it was good for him, sooner or later, and to turn it away from him if it was harmful to him, sooner or later. This is his need which he asked for. Nothing remained for him except contentment with what He decrees for him. So he said: "Decree for me the good wherever it may be, then make me content with it."

This supplication includes these divine knowledges and faith-based realities, among which are trust and entrusting before the occurrence of what is decreed, and contentment after it. Contentment is the fruit of trust, and entrusting is the sign of its soundness. If he is not content with what has been decreed for him, then his entrusting is flawed and corrupt.

By completing these eight levels, the servant completes the station of trust and his foot is firmly established in it. This is the meaning of the saying of Bishr al-Hafi: one of them says, "I have put my trust in Allah," and he lies against Allah. If he had truly trusted in Allah, he would be content with what Allah does to him.

And the saying of Yahya ibn Mu'adh, when he was asked: when does a man become one who trusts? He said: when he is content with Allah as his trustee.

If it is said: since the entire affair belongs to Allah, and the servant has no share in the affair at all, how does the owner appoint a trustee over his own possession, and how does he delegate to him what belongs to him, without this trustee? When the elect (khassa) realized this, they descended from the station of trust and handed it over to the common people (amma), and the address concerning trust remained for them, not for the elect.

It is said: since the entire affair belongs to Allah, mighty and majestic, and the servant has no share in it at all, his trust in Allah is the surrender of the affair to the one to whom it belongs, the removal of himself from the disputes of its owner, his reliance upon Him in it, and his departure from acting by himself, by his own power, strength, and existence, to acting by his Lord and existing by Him, glorified is He, rather than by his own self. This is the intended aim of trust.

As for the servant's removal of himself from the station of trust, it is the removal of himself from the reality of servitude.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 5, verse 23 (part 3 of 4):

As for the address of this (verse) to the common people: Glory be to God! Did God address trust (tawakkul, complete reliance upon God) in His Book except to His elite servants, the closest to Him and the most honoured by Him? He made their faith conditional upon their being trusting, and whatever is conditional on a condition ceases to exist when that condition is absent.

This indicates that faith is absent when trust is absent. Whoever has no trust has no faith. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And upon God rely, if you are believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And upon God let the believers rely﴾ [Al 'Imran: 122]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The believers are only those who, when God is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely﴾ [al-Anfal: 2].

This indicates that the believers are restricted to those who have this attribute.

God, exalted is He, informed about His messengers that trust was their refuge and their shelter. He commanded it to His Messenger in four places in His Book. He said: ﴿And Musa said, "O my people, if you have believed in God, then upon Him rely, if you are Muslims." They said, "Upon God we rely"﴾ [Yunus: 84]. So how could it be among the weakest of means when this is its status? And God, glorified and exalted, knows best.

[Section: The Degrees of Trust]

[The First Degree: Trust with Seeking]

He said: It has three degrees, all of which follow the way of the common people. The first degree: trust together with seeking and taking up the means (sabab, the causal means), with the intention of occupying the self with the means out of fear (of idleness), benefiting people, and abandoning claims (to merit).

He says: The person of this degree relies upon God, and does not abandon the means. Rather, he engages with them with the intention of occupying the self with the means, fearing that if it is left idle, it will busy itself with desire and worldly pleasures. If he does not occupy his self with what benefits it, it will occupy him with what harms him. This is especially so when idleness is combined with the vigour of youth, the possession of vitality, the inclination of the self towards desire, and the succession of heedlessness. As it has been said:

Youth, idleness, and vitality
are a corruption to a man, what a corruption!

And his engagement with the means may also be with the intention of benefiting himself and benefiting people through it. Thus he gains the benefit of himself and the benefit of others.

As for its including the abandonment of claims: when he engages with the means, he is freed from people's attention towards him, which would cause him to think well of himself, and this would lead to his claims. So the means is a veil over his state and his station, and a curtain let down over him.

And from another aspect: he witnesses through it his poverty and humbleness, and his degradation like the degradation of slaves and labourers. Thus he is freed from the foolishness of the self's claims, for when he humbles his self by engaging with the means, he is saved from these diseases.

It is said: If the means are commanded, then there is in them a benefit greater than these three. That is what is intended primarily, while these (three) are intended as secondary aims. That is the establishment of servitude ('ubudiyyah) and the matter for which the servant was created, for which the messengers were sent, and for which the books were revealed. By it the heavens and the earth stand, and for it Paradise and Hell were created.

So engaging with the commanded means is pure servitude, and it is God's right upon His servant, towards which the demands are directed, and upon which reward and punishment are based. And God, glorified is He, knows best.

[Section: The Second Degree: Trust with Dropping Seeking]

He said: The second degree: trust together with dropping seeking, and lowering the gaze from the means, striving to correct trust, suppressing the nobility of the self, and devoting oneself to the preservation of obligations.

His saying: "together with dropping seeking" means: from creation, not from the Truth. So he does not ask anything from anyone. This is among the finest and most beneficial statements for the seeker (murid). For seeking from creation is essentially forbidden, and at most it is permitted in cases of necessity, like the permission of carrion for one who is compelled. Ahmad stated that it is not obligatory. Likewise our shaykh used to indicate that seeking and asking are not obligatory.

I heard him say about asking: It is an injustice against the right of Lordship, an injustice against the right of creation, and an injustice against the self.

As for the injustice against the right of Lordship: it contains humbling oneself before other than God, spilling the honour of one's face for other than one's Creator, substituting asking Him with asking creatures, and exposing oneself to His displeasure when one asks while He has what suffices him for his day.

As for the injustice against people: it is competing with them over what is in their hands by asking, and extracting it from them. The thing most hated by them is one who asks them for what is in their hands, and the thing most loved by them is one who does not ask them. For their wealth is what they love, and whoever asks you for what you love has exposed himself to your hatred and dislike.

As for the injustice of the asker to his own self: it lies in humiliating it and placing it in the station of the humiliation of asking. He is content for it to be humbled by seeking from one who is like himself, or perhaps the asker is better than him and higher in rank. He abandons asking the One of whom it is said: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. So the asker has placed his self in the station of humiliation and degraded it thereby. He is content to be a beggar begging from another beggar like himself, for whomever you beg is also a beggar like you. God alone is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.

So one creature's asking of another creature is the asking of a poor man from a poor man. The Lord, exalted is He, whenever you ask Him, you are honoured in His sight, and He is pleased with you and loves you. And the creature, whenever you ask him, you are humbled in his sight, and he hates you, dislikes you and detests you, as it has been said:

God is angered if you leave off asking Him,
and the sons of Adam are angered when they are asked.

It is ugly for the desiring servant to expose himself to asking servants, while he finds with his Master everything he desires. In Sahih Muslim, from 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), nine, or eight, or seven of us, and he said: 'Will you not pledge allegiance to the Messenger of God?' We had only recently given a pledge. We said: 'We have pledged allegiance to you, O Messenger of God.' Then he said: 'Will you not pledge allegiance to the Messenger of God?' So we extended our hands and said: 'We have pledged allegiance to you, O Messenger of God; upon what should we pledge allegiance to you?' He said: 'That you worship God, and do not associate anything with Him, and the five prayers'—and he said a word quietly—'and that you do not ask people for anything.' He said: 'I have seen some of those people, when the whip of one of them fell, he would not ask anyone to hand it to him.'"

And in the two Sahihs, from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "A person will not cease asking until he meets God with no piece of flesh on his face."

And in both of them also from him: "That the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said—while he was on the pulpit, and mentioned charity and abstaining from asking—'The upper hand is better than the lower hand. The upper hand is the giving hand, and the lower hand is the asking hand.'"

And in Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever asks people to increase his wealth, he is only asking for live coals. So let him make it little or let him make it much."

And in al-Tirmidhi, from Samurah ibn Jundub, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Asking is a scraping by which a man scrapes his face, except that a man asks a ruler, or about a matter that is unavoidable." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a sound hadith.

And in it, from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, as a raised (marfu') hadith: "Whoever is struck by poverty and then brings it upon people, his poverty will not be relieved. And whoever brings it upon God, God will soon provide him with sustenance, sooner or later."

And in the Sunan and the Musnad, from Thawban, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever guarantees to me that he will not ask people for anything, I guarantee him Paradise." I said: "I will." So he did not ask anyone for anything.

And in Sahih Muslim, from Qabisah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Asking is not lawful except for one of three: a man who has undertaken a financial obligation of compensation, for which asking is lawful for him until he obtains it, then he should refrain. And a man struck by a calamity that has wiped out his wealth, for whom asking is lawful until he obtains sufficient sustenance—or he said: a adequate livelihood. And a man struck by poverty until three wise people from his people say: 'Such-and-such has been struck by poverty,' then asking is lawful for him until he obtains sufficient sustenance—or he said: an adequate livelihood. Other than these, O Qabisah, asking is unlawful gain, which its possessor consumes as unlawful gain."

So trust together with dropping this seeking and asking is pure servitude.

His saying: "and lowering the gaze from causation, striving to correct trust." Its meaning: he turns away from occupying himself with the means, in order to correct trust by testing the self. For one who engages with the means may think that he has attained trust, yet he has not attained it, because of his confidence in what he knows. So when he turns away from the means, his trust becomes sound.

This is the view that this (statement) points to, held by a group of worshippers and wayfarers. Many of them used to enter the desert without provisions, and considered carrying provisions a flaw in trust. They have famous stories about this. These people are under the protection of their sincerity, but otherwise their rank is lacking compared to the knowers. Even so, it is absolutely impossible for a human to abandon the means entirely.

Thus Ibrahim al-Khawwas was stringent in trust, examining it closely. He would enter the desert without provisions, and he never parted with a needle, thread, water-vessel, or scissors. He was asked: "Why do you carry this while you forbid everything?" He said: "Such things do not diminish trust, because God has obligations upon us. A poor man has only one garment, and perhaps it tears. If he has no needle and thread, his nakedness may be exposed, and his prayer would be spoiled. If he has no water-vessel, his purification would be spoiled. If you see a poor man without a water-vessel, needle, or thread, then suspect him regarding his prayer."

Do you not see that his religion was not upright except through the means? Is not the movement of his feet and their transport along the road, and seeking guidance by its markers—if they become obscure to him—among the means?

So abstaining from means entirely is impossible by reason, by revelation, and by sense.

Yes, sometimes there comes upon the truthful one a strength of trust in God, and a state with God that moves him to abandon every means that is obligatory upon him, just as it moves him to cast himself into places of destruction. That moment is by God, not by himself. Then a support from God comes to him according to the requirement of his state. But this state does not endure for him, and it is not according to the nature of human beings. It was a sudden onslaught that came upon him without his summoning it, so he yielded to it. If he summons its like and forces himself to it, he will not be answered in that. In that state, if he abandons the means, he is excused because of the strength of the incoming state and his inability to occupy himself with the means. So in his incoming state there is help for him, and it carries him. But if he attempts that state without that incoming state, he falls into the (wrong) state.

As for all those sound stories told about the people, they are particular events that happened to them at times. They are not a path commanded to be followed, nor are they within one's capacity. They became a trial for two groups.

One group thought them a path and a station, so they acted upon them. Some of them ceased, some of them returned, and they could not persist upon them, but turned back on their heels.

Another group criticised their people, and made them opponents of the Shari'ah and reason, claiming for themselves a state more perfect than the state of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his Companions, since none of them ever did that, nor neglected any of the means. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) "wore two coats of mail on the day of Uhud." He never entered the line naked, as one does who has no knowledge and no understanding. He hired a polytheist guide who followed the religion of his people, to guide him on the route of the Migration. God guided the worlds through him, and protected him from all people. "He used to store for his family a year's provisions," and he was the master of the trusting. Whenever he travelled on jihad, or Hajj, or 'Umrah, he carried provisions, water-skins, and all his Companions, and they were truly the people of trust.

The most perfect of those who trust in God after them is one who catches the scent of their trust from a great distance, or who follows a trace of their dust. The state of the Prophet ﷺ and the state of his Companions are the touchstone of states and their balance; by them the sound is known from the sick. Their aspirations in trusting God were higher than the aspirations of those who came after them. Their trust was in opening the insights of hearts, in that God be worshipped in all lands, that all servants should affirm His oneness, and that the suns of the true religion should shine upon the hearts of servants. So they filled hearts with guidance and faith through that trust, and they opened the lands of disbelief and made them abodes of faith. The breezes of the fragrant winds of trust blew upon the hearts of their followers and filled them with certainty and faith. The aspirations of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, were too high and too noble for any of them to direct the strength of his trust and reliance upon God toward something that is attained with minimal stratagem and effort, placing it before his eyes and bending the powers of his trust toward it.

His saying: "and suppressing the nobility of the self." He means that the one who takes up a means may be engaged, through means, in noble governorships for worship, or in exalted trades, and in the causes by which he has standing and honour among people. When he abandons them, his abandonment is a suppression of the nobility of his self and a preference for humility.

And his saying: "and devoting oneself to preserving obligations"; that is, by abandoning them he devotes himself to preserving the obligations that those means would crowd out. And God knows best.

[Section: The Third Degree: Trust Together with Knowledge of Trust]

He said: The third degree: trust together with knowledge of trust, which tends toward release from the cause of trust. It is that one knows that God the Exalted's dominion over things is a dominion of might, in which no partner shares with Him. So he entrusts his partnership to Him. For it is a necessity of servanthood that the servant know that the Real, glorified is He, alone is the Owner of things.

He means that the possessor of this degree, when he cuts off the means and the seeking, and transcends those two degrees, his trust surpasses the trust of those before him. This occurs only after his knowledge of the reality of trust, and that it is lower than his station. So his knowledge of it and of its reality becomes "tending" (nazi'ah), that is, prompting and calling, toward his release from the cause of trust. That is, one does not know the cause of trust until he knows its reality. Then he knows trust with the knowledge that calls him to free himself from its cause.

Then he explained the knowledge by which one knows the cause of trust. He said: that one knows that the Real's dominion over things is a dominion of might; that is, a dominion of inaccessibility, power and subjugation, which prevents any partner from sharing in His dominion over any of things. He is the Mighty in His dominion, from Whom no other shares even an atom. Just as He is the one alone in His might, in which no partner shares.

So the one who trusts sees that he has something in which he has entrusted the Real, and that He, glorified is He, has become his agent concerning it. This contradicts the reality of the matter, since no one has any share of the affair alongside God. Therefore he said: "no partner shares in it." So he entrusts his partnership to Him. The state of affairs says to one who has made the Lord the Exalted his agent: In what have you entrusted your Lord? Is it in what belongs to Him alone? Or to you alone? Or between you both? The second and third are impossible, given His sole ownership of the dominion. And entrusting in the first is impossible; so how would you entrust Him with what you have no share in at all?

It is said: here are two matters: trust (tawakkul) and entrustment (tawkil). Trust is pure reliance, confidence and tranquillity toward the One to whom the whole affair belongs. The servant's knowledge of the Real, the Exalted's sole singularity in owning all things, and that He has no partner in any atom of existence, is among the strongest causes of his trust and the greatest of its motives.

When this is realized in knowledge and recognition, and it touches his heart as a state, he finds no alternative to his heart's reliance upon the Real alone, its confidence in Him alone, its tranquillity toward Him alone, and its peace in Him alone, knowing that his needs, his poverty, his necessities, and all his interests are in His hand alone, not in the hand of another. Then where would his heart find an escape from trust after this?

So the cause of trust at that point is the heart's turning toward one who has no share in the dominion of the Real, and who does not own an atom's weight in the heavens or on earth. This is the cause of his trust. He works to purify his trust from this cause.

Yes, and there is another cause: the seeing of one's own trust, for that is a turning toward the worlds of one's self.

And a third cause: directing the strength of one's trust toward something other than Him which is more beloved to God than it.

These three causes are the causes of entrustment.

As for trust, its meaning is nothing but mere delegation (tafwid), which is among the most distinctive stations of the knowers. As the Prophet ﷺ used to say: "O God, I have submitted my soul to You, and I have committed my affair to You." And God the Exalted said of the believer of Pharaoh's family: ﴿And I commit my affair to God; indeed God is Seeing of the servants﴾ [Ghafir: 44].

The reward of this delegation was His saying: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they schemed﴾ [Ghafir: 45]. If trust is conditioned by what he mentioned, then delegation is likewise so. And it is not so.

Were it not that the truth belongs to God and His Messenger, and that everything other than God and His Messenger is taken from his words and left, and is subject to illusion and error, we would not have objected to those whose dust we cannot reach, nor run in their course, and whom we see above us in the stations of faith and the abodes of travellers, like shining stars. Whoever has knowledge, let him guide us to it. Whoever sees in our words deviation, or deficiency and error, let him guide us to the right. We thank him for his effort, and we receive it with acceptance, submission, compliance and surrender. And God knows best, and He is the Granter of success.

(Section)

Then reflect upon a wondrous wisdom: though beasts, wild animals, predators and creeping things are so numerous, not one of them is seen dead, and they are not a small number that would be hidden by their scarcity. Indeed, it has been said that they outnumber mankind. Consider this from what you see in the deserts: herds of gazelles, cattle, wild goats, wolves, leopards, many kinds of insects of every sort, all other land animals, and types of birds, which are multiples upon multiples of the sons of Adam, yet you can hardly see any of them dead, neither in their resting places, nor in their nests, nor in their falling places, nor in their pastures, paths, watering places, resting stations, refuges, or hiding places, except for those that were overtaken by an attack: either a predator seized it, or a hunter shot it, or an enemy attacked it and occupied it and its kind, preventing them from securing its body and concealing its carcass. This shows that when they sense death and cannot overcome it, they hide themselves where their bodies cannot be reached, and they bury their carcasses before the separation (death) comes upon them. Were it not so, the deserts would be filled with their carcasses and the air would be corrupted by their smells; the harm of that would return upon people and it would become a cause of plague. This is also indicated by the words of Allah the Exalted in the story of the two sons of Adam: ﴿Then Allah sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to conceal the corpse of his brother. He said, "Woe to me! Am I unable to be like this crow and conceal the corpse of my brother?" And he became among the regretful.﴾

As for why its life among people is like that of cattle and beasts of burden, this is because of man's ability to transport it and his cunning in averting its harm, which prevents what has been placed in wild animals such as predators. So reflect on this matter in which the children of Adam are perplexed, and on what they do with it: how it was made a natural instinct in animals, and how they learned it from birds.

Reflect also upon the wisdom in Allah the Exalted sending to the son of Adam a crow, whose name announces the estrangement of the killer from his brother, and whose own estrangement is a mercy of Allah the Exalted: his estrangement from his father and family, and his feeling of strangeness from them and their feeling of strangeness from him.

It is one of the birds from which people shrink and at whose cawing they feel uneasy, so Allah sent to him such a bird until it became like a teacher and a master to him, and he became like a student and one who learns. Do not deny the wisdom of this principle and the connection between names and what they denote, for the Prophet ﷺ said: "When you send a messenger to me, send one with a good name and a good face."

He (ﷺ) used to ask about the name of a land when he alighted in it and the name of a person when he came to him. When Suhayl ibn Amr came to them on the day of Hudaybiyah, he said: "Your affair has become easy (sahl)." And when he wanted to change the name Hazn to Sahl, he said: "The meaning of its name will remain in him and in his descendants."

When Umar ibn al-Khattab asked a man about his name, his father's name, his house and his dwelling, he informed him that he was Jamrah ibn Shihab, that his house was in al-Harqah, and that his dwelling was from it, Dhat Lazha. He said to him: "Check your house, for it has burned," and so it was as he said.

The examples of this principle are too many to mention here. This is a subtle line of inquiry and a very close correspondence between names and their effects. People, past and present, have often been fond of the cawing of the crow and used it as evidence of separation and estrangement; they attribute ill omen to it and shun it, and it shuns them. So it was fitting that this bird should be sent to the killer of the two sons of Adam rather than any other bird, as if it were an image of his own bird, which he had bound around his neck and which flew away from his deed. Do not think that the sending of the crow occurred by chance, devoid of wisdom. If the aspect of wisdom is hidden from you, do not deny it; know that its concealment comes from its subtlety and nobility. And Allah the Exalted, in what hides the aspect of wisdom from humankind, has manifest decrees containing praiseworthy ends.

**Section**

**Type six: mention of what is an explicit statement of cause, using *min ajl* (because of).** An example is His saying: ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had slain all of mankind﴾.

Some have thought that His saying ﴿because of that﴾ gives the cause for His saying ﴿and he became of the regretful﴾, meaning: because of his killing of his brother. This is nothing, for it disturbs the soundness of the composition, diminishes the benefit of mentioning it, and removes the significance of giving the cause for the prescription mentioned, and the magnifying of the gravity of killing, since it is made the cause for this prescription. So reflect on it.

If you say: How can one child of Adam's killing of another be the cause for His ruling on another nation with that same ruling? And if it is a cause, how can the killer of one soul be in the position of the killer of all people?

I say: The Lord, glorified is He, makes His decrees and His predestinations causes and reasons for His legislation and His command. So He made His cosmic, predestined ruling a cause for His religious, commanding ruling. This is because killing, in His sight, since it is among the highest kinds of wrongdoing and corruption, He glorified its matter and magnified its significance, and made its sin greater than the sin of others, and placed the killer of one soul in the position of the killer of all souls.
