It does not follow from a comparison that the compared thing must be in the position of that to which it is compared in every respect. If the killer of all souls will burn in the Fire, and the killer of one soul will also burn in it, then the comparison is valid, just as one who drinks a single drop of wine is sinful, and one who drinks many qintars (large measures) is sinful, even though the amount of sin differs. Likewise, one who commits adultery once and another who commits it many times are both sinful, even though the degree of sin differs. This is the meaning of the statement of Mujahid: "Whoever kills one soul will burn in the Fire for killing it, just as one who kills all people will burn in it."

On this basis, the comparison is in the basic punishment, not in its description. If you wish, you may say the comparison is in the basic worldly penalty and its measure, for it does not differ by the fewness or the multitude of the killing, just as if one drinks a single drop, his legal punishment is the punishment of one who drinks a whole waterskin, and one who commits adultery with one woman receives the same legal punishment as one who commits it with a thousand. This is the interpretation of al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd, who said: "He must undergo retaliation (qisas) for killing it, the same as what he would owe if he had killed all people." You may also make the comparison in the harm and distress that reach the believers through the killing of one of them, for he has made them all his adversaries and inflicted upon them harm and distress resembling killing. This is the interpretation of Ibn al-Anbari. There are other interpretations of the verse.

**[Section: The Crime of Killing]**

Since the corruption of killing is this great, Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had slain all of mankind; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all of mankind﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 32].

The understanding of this has been confused for many people, and they said: It is known that the sin of one who kills a hundred is greater before Allah than the sin of one who kills a single soul. They were led to this because they assumed that the comparison concerns the amount of sin and punishment, but the wording does not indicate this, and comparing one thing to another does not require taking it with all its rulings.

Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿As if on the day they see it, they had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 46].

And He, exalted is He, has said: ﴿As if on the day they see what they are promised, they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35].

This does not mean that their remaining in the world was only this amount.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever prays the 'Isha' in congregation, it is as if he had stood (in prayer) for half the night, and whoever prays the Fajr in congregation, it is as if he had stood the whole night." That is, together with the 'Isha, as occurs in another wording. And more explicit than this is his saying: "Whoever fasts Ramadan and follows it with six (days) of Shawwal, it is as if he had fasted the whole time (al-dahr)." And his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, it is as if he had recited a third of the Qur'an." It is known that the reward of the doer of these deeds does not reach the reward of that to which they are compared, so the two would not be equal in measure. If the measure of reward were equal, there would be no benefit for one who prays 'Isha and Fajr in congregation in the night prayer except fatigue and exertion. No one has been given, after faith, anything better than understanding from Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills.

If it is said: In what respect does the comparison occur between the killer of one soul and the killer of all people?

It is said: In several aspects.

The first: that each of them disobeys Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ), opposes His command, and exposes himself to His punishment. Each of them has earned the wrath and curse of Allah, the deserving of eternal dwelling in the Fire of Hell, and the preparation for him of a great punishment. The difference lies only in the degrees of punishment. The sin of one who kills a prophet, or a just leader, or a scholar who commands people to justice, is not like the sin of one who kills someone who has no distinction among ordinary people.

The second: that they are equal in deserving the taking of a soul's life.

The third: that they are equal in boldness toward shedding forbidden blood, for one who kills a soul without right, merely for the sake of corruption in the land or to take its property, is audacious toward killing everyone he can overpower and manage to kill. He is an enemy of the human species.

Among them: that he is called a killer, or a sinner, or a wrongdoer, or a disobedient one, by killing one, just as he is so called by killing all people.

Among them: that Allah, glorified is He, made the believers, in their mutual affection, mercy, and connection, like one body: if one limb of it complains, the rest of the body responds to it with fever and sleeplessness. So when the killer destroys a limb of this body, it is as if he has destroyed the whole body and caused pain to all its limbs. Whoever harms one believer, it is as if he harms all the believers, and in harming all the believers there is harm to all people, for Allah defends people through the believers who are among them. Harming the protector is harming the one he protects. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No soul is killed unjustly without right, but that there falls upon the first son of Adam a share of it, because he was the first to establish killing."

This threat did not come concerning the first adulterer, nor the first thief, nor the first drinker of intoxicants, though the first of the polytheists may be more deserving of this than the first killer, because he was the first to establish polytheism. For this reason, the Prophet (ﷺ) saw 'Amr ibn Luhayy al-Khuza'i being punished with the greatest punishment in the Fire, because he was the first to change the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41].

That is, those who come after you will follow you, so the sin of their disbelief will be upon you. The same ruling applies to whoever establishes a bad practice that is then followed.

In Jami' al-Tirmidhi, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The one who was killed will come on the Day of Resurrection, with his forehead and head in his hand, and his veins gushing blood, saying: 'O Lord, ask this one: for what did he kill me?'" They mentioned to Ibn 'Abbas the matter of repentance, so he recited this verse: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Nisa': 93].

Then he said: This verse has not been abrogated (naskh) nor replaced, and how could he have repentance? Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a good (hasan) hadith.

Also in it, from Nafi', who said: One day 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar looked at the Ka'bah and said: "How great you are, and how great is your sanctity! Yet the believer is greater in sanctity before Allah than you." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a good hadith.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Samurah ibn Jundub, who said: "The first part of a person to rot is his belly, so whoever among you can eat only what is good, let him do so, and whoever can prevent a handful of blood he has spilled from coming between him and Paradise, let him do so."

Also in his Sahih, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The believer remains in latitude in his religion as long as he has not shed forbidden blood."

Al-Bukhari also mentioned, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: Among the calamities of matters from which there is no escape for one who casts himself into them is the shedding of forbidden blood without its lawful right.

In the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Reviling a believer is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief."

In the two of them also, from him (ﷺ): "Do not revert after me to disbelief, striking one another's necks."

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from him (ﷺ): "Whoever kills a mu'ahad (one under covenant) will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance is found from a distance of forty years."

This is the punishment of one who kills an enemy of Allah while he is under a covenant and safe-conduct. So what is the punishment of one who kills His believing servant? And if a woman entered the Fire because of a cat she imprisoned until it died of hunger and thirst, and the Prophet (ﷺ) saw her in the Fire while the cat was scratching her face and chest, then what is the punishment of one who imprisons a believer until he dies without any crime? And in some of the Sunan, from him (ﷺ): "The disappearance of the world is less significant to Allah than the killing of a believer without right."

The punishment that Allah has prescribed for one who spreads fear on the road and cuts off the highway is this: his limbs are cut off, and every route is cut off to him by exile from the land, so that he travels in it only in fear.

[Section: The Repentance of the Hirabah-Offender (al-muharib)]

As for considering the repentance of the muharib (one who wages war against society by highway robbery) before he is captured, to the exclusion of others, it is said: where in the texts of the Lawgiver is this distinction? Rather, his explicit ruling on considering the repentance of the muharib before he is captured is either by way of alerting to the consideration of the repentance of others by a stronger argument (bab al-tanbih ala i'tibar tawbat ghayrihi bi-tariq al-awla). For if his repentance averts from him the prescribed penalty for his hirabah despite its great harm and its aggression, then repentance averting what falls short of the penalty for hirabah is all the more deserved and more fitting. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, they will be forgiven what has already passed﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]. The Prophet ﷺ said: "One who repents from sin is like one who has no sin." Allah the Exalted has made the hudud (prescribed punishments, sing. hadd) a penalty for the perpetrators of crimes, and He has lifted the penalty from the repentant, both by the Law and by Divine decree. Therefore there is no punishment of a penitent in Allah's Law or His decree whatsoever.

In the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of Anas, who said: "I was with the Prophet ﷺ when a man came and said: O Messenger of Allah, I have committed a hadd offence, so establish it upon me. He did not ask him about it. Then the prayer came, and he prayed with the Prophet ﷺ. When the Prophet ﷺ finished the prayer, the man came to him and repeated his statement. He said: 'Did you not pray with us?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forgiven you your sin.'" So this man, when he came repentant of his own accord without being sought, was forgiven by Allah, and the hadd for what he had confessed was not established upon him. This is one of the two opinions on the question, and it is one of the two narrations from Ahmad, and it is the correct view.

If it is said: Ma'iz came repentant, and the Ghamidiyya came repentant, and the hadd was established upon both of them.

It is said: there is no doubt that both came repentant, and there is no doubt that the hadd was established upon both of them, and by them the proponents of the other opinion argued. I asked our Shaykh about this, and he answered with what amounts to this: the hadd is purifying, and repentance is purifying, and both of them chose purification through the hadd over purification through repentance alone, and they refused except to be purified by the hadd. The Prophet ﷺ granted them that, and guided toward choosing purification through repentance over purification through the hadd. Regarding Ma'iz he said: "Why did you not leave him, so that he might repent and Allah might accept his repentance?" Had the hadd been definitively required after repentance, it would not have been permissible to abandon it; rather the Imam has the choice between abandoning it, as he said to the owner of the hadd who confessed: "Go, for Allah has forgiven you," and between establishing it, as he established it upon Ma'iz and the Ghamidiyya when they chose its establishment and refused except to be purified by it. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ turned them away repeatedly while they insisted on its establishment upon them. This path is the middle course between the path of one who says it is not permissible to establish it after repentance at all, and the path of one who says repentance has no effect whatsoever in dropping it. And if you reflect upon the Sunnah, you will find that it indicates nothing but this middle opinion. And Allah knows best.

[Section: Cutting off (the hand) for corrupting wealth]

He, glory be to Him, made the cutting off (of the hand) correspond to the corruption of wealth, which cannot be guarded against, because the thief takes wealth by stealth, breaks into houses, and climbs over walls rather than using the doors. He is like the cat and the snake that enter upon you from where you do not know. The harm of his theft does not rise to the level of killing, nor is it averted by flogging. The best way to repel his harm is to remove the limb with which he exercises his aggression, and flogging was made to correspond to the corruption of minds and the tearing of honour through slander.

Thus His legislated punishments, glory be to Him, revolve around these three types, just as the expiations (kaffarat) revolve around three types: manumission, which is the highest of them, feeding, and fasting.

(A subtle point)

Some Arabs heard a reciter recite: ﴿And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, a punishment from Allah﴾ [and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful]. He said: "This is not the speech of Allah, the Exalted."

The reciter said: "Do you deny the speech of Allah, the Exalted?!"

He said: "No, but this is not the speech of Allah." So the reciter returned to his memorization and recited: ﴿And Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾.

The Bedouin said: "You have spoken the truth. He is Mighty, so He decreed, and so He cut off. Had He forgiven and shown mercy, He would not have cut off."

For this reason, when a verse of mercy is concluded with the name of punishment, or vice versa, the discord of the speech and its lack of coherence becomes apparent.

(Section)

Since the motive for theft is strong and its corruption is likewise great, He cut off the hand for it.

Consider His wisdom in corrupting the limb with which the offence was carried out, just as He corrupted the hands and feet of the highwayman, which are the instruments of his offence. He did not corrupt the tongue of the slanderer with which he committed his offence, since its harm exceeds the harm of the offence without reaching it; so He was content, in that case, with inflicting pain on his whole body through flogging.

If it is said: "Why did He not corrupt the sexual organ of the fornicator, with which he committed the sin?"

It is answered: For several reasons.

First: the harm of that exceeds the harm of the offence, since it involves cutting off offspring and exposing them to destruction.

Second: the private part is a concealed organ, and cutting it does not achieve the purpose of the hadd, which is deterrence and restraint for others like the offenders, unlike the cutting of the hand.

Third: when he cuts off the hand, a second hand remains to compensate for it, unlike the private part.

Fourth: the pleasure of fornication pervades the whole body, so it is better that the punishment pervade the whole body, and this is more fitting than restricting it to a piece of the body.

Thus the punishments of the Lawgiver came in the most complete forms, the most conformable to reason, and the most upright in their benefit.

The point is that sins are followed by punishments, either legislated, or decreed by destiny, or Allah gathers them upon the servant; and He may lift them from one who repents and does good.

[Section: The difference between the hand in blood money and the hand in theft]

As for cutting off the hand for a quarter of a dinar, and making its blood money five hundred dinars, this is among the greatest of benefits and wisdom. He was cautious in both cases regarding wealth and limbs: He cut it for a quarter of a dinar to preserve wealth, and made its blood money five hundred dinars to preserve and safeguard it. Some heretics (zanadiqa) raised this question and expressed it in two verses:

"A hand whose blood money was valued at five hundred of gold,
why was it cut off for a quarter of a dinar?
A contradiction; we have nothing but silence about it,
and we seek refuge in our Master from shame."

Some jurists answered it: it was precious when it was trustworthy; when it betrayed, it became worthless. The versifier expressed it as:

"A hand whose blood money was valued at five hundred of gold,
yet it was cut off for a quarter of a dinar.
Protecting blood is what makes it costly and cheap:
the betrayal of wealth. So consider the wisdom of the Creator."

It is related that al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, answered with his words:

"There, a wronged one whose value was exalted;
here, one who wronged, and became worthless before the Creator."

Shams al-Din al-Kurdi answered with his words:

"Say to al-Ma'arri: shame, what a shame,
the ignorance of a youth, while he is shamefully devoid of the garment of piety.
Do not strike the flint of poetry for wisdoms;
the symbols of the Law have not been kindled by verses.
So the value of a hand is half a thousand of gold,
but if it transgresses, it is not worth a dinar."

[Section: The difference between the thief and the plunderer]

As for cutting off the hand of the thief for three dirhams, and leaving aside cutting off the hand of the one who snatches, the plunderer and the usurper, this too is part of the complete wisdom of the Lawgiver. The thief cannot be guarded against, for he breaks into houses, tears open the protected place, and breaks the lock, and the owner of the goods cannot guard himself beyond that. Had He not legislated cutting for him, people would steal from one another, the harm would grow, and the tribulation caused by thieves would intensify. This is unlike the plunderer and the snatcher: the plunderer is one who takes property openly, in the sight of people, so people can seize his hands, rescue the right of the wronged, or testify for him before the judge. As for the snatcher, he takes property only in a moment of heedlessness on the part of its owner and others, and so there is always some kind of negligence that enables the snatcher to snatch. Without it, with full vigilance and alertness, he cannot snatch. Thus he is not like the thief; rather he is more like the betrayer. Also, the snatcher generally takes property from outside its usual protected place, for he is the one who catches you off guard and snatches your goods while you are away from them and inattentive to guarding them, and this can generally be guarded against; so he is like the plunderer. As for the usurper, the matter is evident, and he is even more deserving of not having his hand cut off than the plunderer. Yet the transgression of these people may be restrained by beating, punishment, long imprisonment, and penalty by taking their property, as will come later.

If it is said: "The Sunnah has come down concerning cutting off the hand of one who denies a loan (ariyya), and its ultimate meaning is that he is a betrayer, and the lender gave him authority over taking his property. Guarding against it is possible by not handing the property over to him; so what you have mentioned of the distinction is refuted."

It is answered: By the life of Allah, the hadith has been authenticated that "a woman used to borrow goods and deny them, so the Prophet ﷺ ordered that her hand be cut off." The jurists differed about the cause of the cutting: was it for her theft? The narrator described her by her attribute, because what is mentioned is the cause of the cutting, as al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Malik say; or was the cause mentioned not the cause of the cutting, as Ahmad and those who agree with him say? In this discussion we do not champion any specific school at all. If the sound view is the view of the majority, the objection is removed. If the sound view is the other opinion, its agreement with analogy, wisdom and benefit is very clear. For lending (ariyya) is among the benefits of the children of Adam which they cannot do without and have no independence from; it is obligatory when the borrower needs it and is in necessity of it, either for a rent or free of charge. The lender cannot be enabled at every moment to call witnesses for the loan, and guarding against it by prohibiting lending is impossible legally, customarily and conventionally. There is no difference in meaning between one who reaches the goods of another by theft and one who reaches them by a loan and then denies it. This is unlike the one who denies a deposit (wadi'a), for the owner of the goods was negligent when he entrusted it to him.

[Section: The wisdom of setting the threshold of theft at a quarter of a dinar]

As for restricting cutting to this amount: a measure is necessary to be a criterion for the obligation of cutting, since one cannot say: one is cut for stealing a fils, or a grain of wheat, or a date. The Law does not come with this, and the wisdom, mercy and benevolence of Allah are too exalted for that. So a criterion is necessary. Three dirhams were the first level of accumulation, and their measure is a quarter of a dinar. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and others among the Followers said: "They did not cut for a trivial thing, for people's custom is to be tolerant regarding a petty thing of their property, since no harm befalls them by its loss." In fixing it at three dirhams there is clear wisdom, for it generally suffices a person of moderate means for his day, for himself and those he supports, and the sustenance of a day for a man and his family is of great concern to most people. There is a well-known report: "Whoever wakes up secure in his dwelling, healthy in his body, with the sustenance of his day, it is as if the whole world has been gathered for him."

[Section: The suspension of the hadd in a year of famine]

The third example: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, suspended the cutting of the thief in a year of famine. Al-Sa'di said: Harun ibn Isma'il al-Khazzaz narrated to us: Ali ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us: Yahya ibn Abi Kathir narrated to me: Hassan ibn Zahir narrated to me that Ibn Huday'r narrated to him from 'Umar, who said: "The hand is not cut off for a palm-cluster nor in a year of drought."

Al-Sa'di said: I asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal about this hadith and he said: "The 'idhq is the palm-tree, and the year of drought is famine." I said to Ahmad: "Do you say this?" He said: "Yes, by my life." I said: "If he steals in a famine, do you not cut him?" He said: "No, when need compels him to that while people are in famine and hardship."

Al-Sa'di said: This is in line with the case of 'Umar regarding the servants of Hatib. Aruma Abu al-Nu'man narrated to us: Hammad ibn Salama narrated to us from Hisham ibn 'Urwa from his father from Ibn Hatib that the servants of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a stole a camel of a man from Muzayna. 'Umar brought them, and they confessed. He sent for 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hatib, and he came, and he said to him: "The servants of Hatib stole a camel of a man from Muzayna and confessed against themselves." 'Umar said: "O Kathir ibn al-Salt, go and cut off their hands." When he turned away with them, 'Umar called them back and said: "By Allah, had I not known that you make them labour and starve them, so that one of them, if he ate what Allah forbade him, it would be lawful for him, I would have cut off their hands. By Allah, if I do not do so, I will fine you a fine that will pain you." Then he said: "O Muzani, for how much was your camel wanted from you?" He said: "For four hundred." 'Umar said: "Go and give him eight hundred."

Ahmad followed 'Umar in both cases together, in the questions of Isma'il ibn Sa'id al-Shalanji, which al-Sa'di explained in a book he named the translator. He said: "I asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal about a man who carries dates from their sheaths, and he said: 'In it there is the price twice, and the punishment of a whip.'" He also said: "Whoever we ward off from him the hadd or retaliation, we double the fine upon him." Al-Awza'i agreed with Ahmad on the suspension of cutting in famine. This is pure analogy and the requirement of the principles of the Law. When the year is a year of famine and hardship, need and necessity overwhelm people, and the thief hardly escapes necessity that drives him to what keeps him alive. The owner of the property is obliged to give him that, either for a price or free of charge, depending on the disagreement on this; the sound view is that it is obligatory to give it free, for the obligation of consolation and preserving souls, when one is able to do so, and of preferring others with surplus over the necessity of the needy. This is a strong doubt that averts cutting from the needy, and it is stronger than many of the doubts that many jurists mention. Indeed, if you weigh this doubt against what they mention, the disparity will appear to you. Where is the doubt that the stolen item is something quickly spoiled, or that its origin is permissible like water, or the doubt of cutting for it once, or the doubt of claiming ownership without evidence, or the doubt of its destruction within the protected place by eating or milking from the udder, or the doubt of the reduction of its value within the protected place by slaughter or burning and then removing it, and other very weak doubts, compared with this strong doubt? Especially since he is permitted to contend with the owner of the property to take what keeps him alive.

The year of famine has many needy and destitute people, and the one who is wealthy among them cannot be distinguished from the thief who steals without need. So the one who is liable to the hadd becomes confused with the one who is not, and so it is averted. Yes, if it becomes clear that the thief has no need and is independent of stealing, he is cut.

[Section: Cutting and what necessitates it]

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 5, verse 38 (part 2 of 3):

As for the amputation, He made it a just punishment for its like and for the punishment of the thief. Its punishment by amputation is more eloquent and more deterrent than its punishment by flogging, and his crime does not reach the level of punishment by killing. So the punishment most fitting for him is the severing of the limb he made a means to harming people and taking their wealth. And since the harm of the one who wages war (muharib) is greater than the harm of the thief, and his transgression is greater, He added to the cutting of his hand the cutting of his foot, in order to restrain his transgression and the evil of his hand with which he strikes and his foot with which he goes about. He also prescribed that this be from opposite sides (khilaf), so that it would not deprive him of the benefit of a whole side. Thus He restrained his harm and transgression, and showed mercy to him by leaving him a hand from one side and a foot from the other side.

[Section: The wisdom in cutting the hand of the thief rather than the tongue of the slanderer (for example)]

As for his saying: "And He cut off the hand of the thief, with which he committed the crime, and did not cut off the private part of the fornicator, though he committed the crime with it, nor the tongue of the slanderer, though he committed the slander with it,"

his answer is that this is among the strongest proofs that this Sharia was sent down from the One who is the Most Wise of judges and the Most Merciful of the merciful.

We will mention a beneficial section on the prescribed penalties (hudud), their measures, the perfection of their ranks according to their causes, and the fact that each offence necessitates what is prescribed for it and not something else, and that beyond this there is no room for the intellects to propose anything. We will also raise questions that this questioner did not raise, and we will answer them, by God's power and might, in the best manner of answering. And God is the One sought for help, and upon Him we rely.

When God, may His praise be exalted and His names be sanctified, created the servants and created death and life, and made what is on the earth an adornment for it, in order to test His servants and try them as to which of them is best in deed, it was not in His wisdom to avoid preparing the causes of the trial within themselves and outside of them. So He placed within them sound intellects, hearing, sight, will, desires, powers, natures, love, hatred, inclination, aversion, and opposing characters, which necessarily produce their effects as a cause necessitates its effect; and outside them are the causes that souls seek to obtain, so they compete for it, and that which they dislike obtaining, so they push it away. Then He reinforced the causes of this trial by appointing over them companions from the wicked, unjust, and corrupt spirits, and companions from the good, just, and pure spirits; and He made the calls and inclinations of the heart fluctuate between the two: it is sometimes inclined to the call of good and sometimes to the call of evil, so that the trial may be completed in the abode of testing, and the wisdom of reward and punishment may appear in the abode of recompense. Both of these are of the Truth by which God created the heavens and the earth, and for which He created them, and they are the requirement of the Lord's dominion and praise. So His dominion and praise must appear in both, just as they appeared in the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. His wisdom, mercy, and justice necessitated, by the judgment of His obligating Himself, that He send His messengers, reveal His books, and prescribe His laws, to complete what His wisdom required in His creation and command, and to establish the market of jihad because of the enmity and discord that arose between these characters, actions, and wills, just as it arose between those in whom they subsist.

So there had to be the realization of what the human natures require, and what accompanies them of causes: rivalry, envy, submission to the calls of desire and anger, transgressing what is set as its limit, and falling short in much of what they are worshipped with. What facilitated this for them was their being deluded by the sources of disobedience while turning away from its outcomes, and their preferring what they hasten to obtain of slight pleasure in their worldly life over what they are deferred of great pleasure in the Hereafter, and their settling on the present that is witnessed, and their turning away from the absent that is promised. This is the necessary result of what they were created upon of ignorance and injustice. Therefore, the Lord's most beautiful names, His highest attributes, His perfect wisdom, His all-encompassing blessing, His all-comprehensive mercy, and His vast generosity required that He not disregard the Reminder from His servants, that He not leave them neglected, and that He not leave them to the calls of their souls and their natures. Rather, He placed in their innate natures and their intellects the knowledge of good and evil, of the beneficial and the harmful, of pain and pleasure, and the knowledge of their causes. He did not suffice with this alone until He made them know it in detail through the tongues of His messengers, and cut off their excuses by establishing, for the truthfulness of His messengers, such proofs and evidences that no argument remains for them against Him, so that whoever perishes perishes upon clear evidence, and whoever lives lives upon clear evidence. Indeed, God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing. He directed for them the paths of promise and threat, of encouragement and warning, struck for them parables, and removed from them every difficulty. He enabled them to carry out what He commanded them and to abandon what He forbade them, to the utmost enablement, and aided them in it by every means, and empowered them to overcome their natures by what leads them to prefer outcomes over beginnings, and to abandon the slight, perishing pleasure for the great, enduring pleasure. He guided them to reflection and contemplation, and to choosing what their intellects and characters judge concerning these two matters. He perfected their religion for them, and completed His blessing upon them by what He conveyed to them through the tongues of His messengers of the causes of punishment and reward, of glad tidings and warning, of desire and dread, and by realizing this partly in the abode of trial as a sign and indication of the realization of what He deferred for them in the abode of recompense and reward; so that the immediate would remind of the deferred, the brief and cut off would point to the abundant and continuous, and the present that passes would announce the absent that endures. Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds, the Most Wise of judges and the Most Merciful of the merciful, and exalted is He above what is supposed of Him by one who has not measured Him, of those who deny His names, attributes, command, prohibition, promise, and threat, and who harbour an evil assumption about Him, so that their assumption destroyed them and they became among the losers.

So it was part of His wisdom and mercy, glory be to Him, that He prescribed penalties for the offences committed between people against one another, against heads, bodies, honour, and wealth, such as killing, wounding, slander, and theft. He perfected the forms of deterrence that repel these offences to the utmost perfection, and prescribed them in the most complete forms that include the interest of deterrence and restraint, while not exceeding what the offender deserves of deterrence. Therefore He did not prescribe for lying the cutting of the tongue, nor for killing, nor for fornication castration, nor for theft the annihilation of the self.

He prescribed for them in this only what is required by His names and attributes: His wisdom, mercy, gentleness, benevolence, and justice, so that calamities would disappear, greed for one another's transgression and aggression would be cut off, and every person would be content with what his Owner and Creator has given him, so that he would not covet the seizing of another's right.

(Section)

[It is not from wisdom to destroy every limb with which a sin was committed]

As for punishing the thief by cutting off his hand and leaving the punishment of the fornicator by cutting off his private part, this is in the utmost wisdom and benefit. It is not in God's wisdom, the welfare of His creation, His care, and His mercy towards them, that He should destroy for every offender every limb with which he disobeyed Him, so that He would prescribe gouging out the eye of one who looked at the forbidden, cutting off the ear of one who listened to it, the tongue of one who spoke with it, or the hand of one who struck another unjustly. There is no concealment of the excess, transgression in punishment, and reversal of its ranks in this; and the Lord's most beautiful names, highest attributes, and praiseworthy acts refuse that. The aim of the Lawgiver is not merely security from recurrence, nothing more. Had this been the aim, he would have killed the perpetrator only. Rather, the aim is restraint, deterrence, and punishment for the offence, and that it be closest to restraining his transgression, that others take warning from him, that the pain he tastes produce in him a sincere repentance, and that it remind him of the punishment of the Hereafter, along with other wisdoms and benefits.

[The wisdom in the prescribed penalty for theft]

Furthermore, in the penalty for theft there is another meaning: theft is only committed by its doer secretly, as its name implies. For this reason they say: "So-and-so looks at so-and-so stealthily (musaraqatan)" when he looks at him with a hidden glance he does not want to be noticed. The one resolved on theft is concealed, hiding, fearful lest his location be perceived and he be seized. Then he is prepared to flee and save himself once he has taken the item. A person's two hands are like the wings of a bird in aiding it to fly. For this reason they say: "I joined the wing of so-and-so" when you see him traveling alone and join him to accompany him. So the thief is punished by cutting off the hand, clipping his wing, and facilitating his capture should he repeat the theft. When this is done to him the first time, he remains with one wing clipped, weak in running. Then in the second offence his foot is cut off, and he becomes even weaker in running, so that he hardly escapes the pursuer. Then his other hand is cut off in the third offence and his other foot in the fourth, so he remains a piece of flesh on a mat, resting and giving rest.

[The categories of sins]

Furthermore, He, glory be to Him, divided sins into three categories:

A category in which there is a prescribed penalty (hadd); for this He did not prescribe expiation (kaffarah), being satisfied with the penalty.

A category for which He did not prescribe a penalty, and so He prescribed expiation for it, such as intercourse during the day in Ramadan, intercourse in the state of ihram, zihar, accidental killing, breaking an oath, and other such things.

A category for which He prescribed neither a penalty nor expiation, and this is of two kinds:

The first: that from which restraint is natural, such as eating feces, drinking urine and blood.

The second: that whose corruption is less than the corruption of what has a prescribed penalty, such as looking, kissing, touching, conversing, stealing a fils, and the like.

The expiations are of three kinds

He prescribed expiations in three kinds:

The first: that which was originally permissible, then its prohibition arose, and one engaged in it in the state in which the prohibition arose, such as intercourse in ihram and fasting. Its counterpart is intercourse during menstruation and post-natal bleeding. Unlike intercourse in the anus; for this reason the attempt of some jurists to equate it with intercourse during menstruation is not valid, since that is not permitted at one time and forbidden at another; rather it is in the position of sodomy and drinking intoxicants.

The second kind: that which is bound to God by a vow, or by God through an oath, or what God has forbidden and then one wishes to make it lawful. God, glory be to Him, prescribed making it lawful again through expiation and called it a gift (nihlah). This expiation is not an erasure of the violation of the sanctity of the Name by breaking the oath, as some jurists supposed; for breaking an oath may be obligatory, may be recommended, and may be permissible. Rather, expiation is only a release from what one bound oneself to.

The third kind: that in which it serves as a compensation for what has been lost, such as the expiation for accidental killing, even if there is no sin there, and the expiation for killing game by mistake. This is of the category of compensations. The first kind is of the category of deterrents, and the middle kind is of the category of release from what the contract was made upon.

(Combining the hadd and ta'zir is not permitted)

The hadd and ta'zir do not combine in one sin. Rather, if there is a hadd in it, one is satisfied with it; otherwise one is satisfied with ta'zir. Likewise, the hadd and expiation do not combine in one sin; rather, every sin that has a hadd has no expiation, and what has an expiation has no hadd. Do ta'zir and expiation combine in a sin that has no hadd?

There are two opinions on this. This is like intercourse in ihram and fasting, and intercourse with a menstruating woman. If we obligate expiation in it, some say ta'zir is obligatory for it, because of the violation of sanctity committed by engaging in the offence; others say there is no ta'zir in that, being satisfied with the expiation because it is a compensation and an erasure.

(Benefit)

The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Jesus saw a man stealing and said: 'Did you steal?' He said: 'No, by Him besides whom there is no god.' Jesus said: 'I believed in God and disbelieved my sight.'" It was said that this is a question from the Messiah, not a statement, and the meaning is: "Did you steal?" and when he swore to him, he believed him. But his saying "and disbelieved my sight" disputes this.

It was also said: when the Messiah saw him, the man was taking property in the form of a thief, so he said: "Did you steal?" He said: "No," meaning it is not theft, either because it is his property or he has a right in it, or because he took it in order to turn it over and return it. The Messiah, peace be upon him, relied on the apparent of what he saw. When he swore to him, he said: "I believed in God and disbelieved myself," in my supposition that it was theft, not that he disbelieved himself in taking the property with his own eyes. So the disbelief falls on the supposition, not on the direct sight. Likewise the narration is "I disbelieved myself."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 5, verse 38 (part 3 of 3):

There is no contradiction between this and the narration "and I disbelieve my eyes," because the eye (al-basar) supposed that this taking was theft, so I (the one who narrates) disbelieved it in its supposition that it had seen theft, whereas perhaps it had only seen a taking that was not theft.

In the hadith there is a third meaning, and it may be the most fitting of them: that the Messiah, peace be upon him, because of the greatness of the reverence and majesty of God in his heart, supposed that this one who swore by the oneness of God, Exalted is He, was truthful. His faith in God caused him to affirm this, and he allowed that his eyes had deceived him and shown him what he had not seen, so he said: "I believed in God and disbelieved my eyes."

There is no doubt that the eye may be subject to error, to seeing some things contrary to what they are, and to imagining what has no existence outside the mind. When the intellect judges against it, its error becomes clear. The Messiah, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, gave precedence to his faith over his sight and attributed the error to it. And God knows best.

And His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom God did not want to purify their hearts﴾, following His saying: ﴿They listen to falsehood, listeners for another people who have not come to you. They distort words from their places﴾.

This shows that when a servant becomes accustomed to listening to falsehood and accepting it, that habit earns him the distortion of the truth from its proper places. When he accepts falsehood, he loves it and is pleased with it. Then when the truth comes contrary to it, he rejects it and denies it if he is able to, and otherwise he distorts it. This is what the Jahmiyya (the followers of Jahm ibn Safwan) do with the verses and hadiths about the divine attributes. They reject these verses through interpretation (ta'wil), which is a denial of their realities, and they reject those hadiths by saying they are reports of single transmitters (akhbar al-ahad), which may not be relied upon in matters of knowing God, His names and His attributes. These people and their like are among those whom God did not want to purify their hearts. For if their hearts had been purified, they would not have turned away from the truth, and would not have substituted falsehood for the words of God and His Messenger. Just as the deviants among the people of spiritual aspiration (ahl al-irada), when their hearts were not purified, substituted satanic listening for faithful Qur'anic listening.

ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan (may God be pleased with him) said: "If our hearts were pure, we would never be satisfied with the words of God."

The pure heart, because of the perfection of its life, its light, and its freedom from defilements and filth, is never satiated with the Qur'an, and is nourished only by its realities and healed only by its remedies. This is unlike the heart which God has not purified, for it is nourished by the foods suited to it, according to the impurity within it.

The impure heart is like a sick, ailing body, to which the foods suited to the healthy body are not agreeable.

The verse shows that the purity of the heart depends on the will of God, and that since He, glory be to Him, did not will to purify the hearts of those who speak falsehood and distort the truth, their hearts did not attain purity.

It is not correct to interpret the will here as the religious will (al-irada al-diniyya), which is the command and the love, for He, glory be to Him, did will this for them as a command and as a love. But He did not will it from them as an existential decree (kawn). So He willed purity for them and commanded them to it, but He did not will its occurrence from them, because of the wisdom He has in that, the loss of which is more hateful to Him than the loss of their purity.

We have fully discussed this in our large book on predestination (al-Qadar).

The verse shows that whoever God does not purify his heart will inevitably be struck with disgrace in this world and punishment in the Hereafter, in proportion to the impurity and corruption of his heart.

For this reason God, glory be to Him, forbade Paradise to whoever has impurity and corruption in his heart, and no one enters it except after being made good and pure.

For it is the abode of the good. That is why they are told: ﴿You are good, so enter it, abiding forever﴾ [al-Zumar: 73].

That is, enter it because of your goodness. And the good tidings at death are for these people and no others, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying: "Peace be upon you. Enter the Garden for what you used to do"﴾ [al-Nahl: 32].

So no corrupt person enters Paradise, nor anyone who has any corruption in him. Whoever purifies himself in this world and meets God pure of his impurities enters it without any hindrance. As for whoever does not purify himself in this world: if his impurity is intrinsic, like that of the disbeliever, he never enters it at all. But if his impurity is acquired and incidental, he enters it after being purified of that impurity in the Fire, and then he comes out of it. Indeed, when the people of faith cross the Bridge (al-Sirat), they are detained on a bridge between Paradise and the Fire, where they are refined and cleansed of remnants that remained upon them, which held them back from Paradise but did not necessitate their entry into the Fire. Then, when they are refined and cleansed, they are given permission to enter Paradise.

God, in His wisdom, made entry into His presence dependent on purity, so one who prays does not enter upon Him until he has purified himself. Likewise, He made entry into His Garden dependent on goodness and purity, so none enters it except the good and pure.

Thus there are two purities: purity of the body and purity of the heart. For this reason it is prescribed for one performing ablution to say after his ablution:

"I bear witness that there is no god but God, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. O God, make me among those who repent, and make me among those who purify themselves."

So the purity of the heart is by repentance, and the purity of the body is by water. When both purities are combined for him, he becomes fit to enter upon God, to stand before Him, and to converse with Him.

I asked Shaykh al-Islam about the meaning of the Prophet's supplication (ﷺ): "O God, purify me of my sins with water, snow and hail."

How are sins purified by that? What is the benefit of specifying these? And his words in another wording, "and cold water," since hot water is more effective in cleansing?

He said: Sins cause the heart heat, impurity and weakness, so the heart becomes slack, and the fire of desire blazes within it and defiles it. Sins and transgressions are to the heart like firewood that feeds the fire and kindles it. That is why, whenever sins multiply, the fire of the heart intensifies and it weakens. Water washes away filth and extinguishes the fire. If it is cold, it gives the body firmness and strength. If it comes with snow and hail, it is stronger in cooling and in firming and strengthening the body, and so it is more effective in removing the traces of sins. This is the meaning of his words, and it needs further explanation and clarification.

Know that there are four matters here: two sensory and two spiritual.

The impurity that is removed by water, and the means of removing it, are both sensory. The traces of sins, which are removed by repentance and seeking forgiveness, and the means of removing them, are both spiritual. The soundness, life and bliss of the heart are achieved only by both of these.

So the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned from each pair a part, thereby alerting to the other part.

Thus his speech comprised the four divisions in the utmost brevity and excellence of explanation.

As in the hadith of the supplication after ablution:

"O God, make me among those who repent, and make me among those who purify themselves."

For it contains mention of the four divisions.

And among the perfection of his eloquence (ﷺ) and his verification of what he informs of and commands is his illustrating an intended spiritual matter by a sensory matter.

This is abundant in his speech, such as his saying in the hadith of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib:

"Ask God for guidance and rectitude (sadad), and remember by guidance your guidance to the road, and by rectitude the rectitude of the arrow."

This is among the most eloquent teaching and counsel, for he commanded that, when asking God for guidance to the path of His pleasure and His Garden, one should recall that he is a traveller who has lost his way and does not know where to head, so a man knowledgeable and experienced in the road appears to him, and he asks him to show him the way. Thus is the state of the path of the Hereafter, illustrated by the sensory road for the traveller. And the traveller's need for God, the Exalted, that He guide him to that path is greater than the traveller's need for someone to show him the route that leads to the destination.

Likewise rectitude (sadad), which is hitting the intended aim in speech and deed. Its likeness is that of the archer: when his arrow falls into the very thing he aimed at, he has made his arrow straight and hit, and it did not fall in vain. Thus is the one who is right in the truth in his speech and deed, like one who hits the mark in his shooting. The Qur'an often combines these two. Among this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And take provision, for the best provision is piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197].

He commanded the pilgrims to take provisions for their journey and not to travel without provision, then He alerted them to the provision for the journey of the Hereafter, which is piety. Just as the traveller cannot reach his destination except with provision that brings him there, so the one travelling to God and the Last Abode cannot arrive except with provision of piety. Thus He combined the two provisions. Among this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your nakedness and as adornment, but the clothing of piety is best﴾ [al-A'raf: 26].

Thus He combined the two adornments: the adornment of the body with clothing and the adornment of the heart with piety, the adornment of the outward and the inward, and the perfection of the outward and the inward. Among this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123].

He negated from him going astray, which is the punishment of the heart and the spirit, and suffering, which is also the punishment of the body and the spirit. So he is blessed in heart and body with guidance and success. Among this is the saying of the wife of al-ʿAziz about Joseph, peace be upon him, when the women who blamed her for loving him showed them his beauty: ﴿That is the one about whom you blamed me﴾ [Yusuf: 32]. So she showed them his outward beauty. Then she said: ﴿I sought to seduce him, but he refused﴾ [Yusuf: 32].

Thus she informed them of his inner beauty by his chastity, and she showed them the beauty of his outward appearance. The Prophet (ﷺ) alerted by his saying: "O God, purify me of my sins with water, snow and hail."

to the great need of the body and the heart for what purifies them, cools them, and strengthens them. His supplication comprised asking for this and that, and God knows best.

Close to this is that when he (ﷺ) came out of the toilet, he would say: "Ghufranaka" (I seek Your forgiveness).

In this there is, and God knows best, a secret: that excrement weighs down the body and harms it by its retention, and sins weigh down the heart and harm it by their retention within it. Both harm and injure the body and the heart. So he praised God upon coming out, for being freed from what harms his body, and for the lightness and ease of the body. And he asked to be freed from the other harm and to have his heart relieved and lightened of it.

The secrets of his words and supplications (ﷺ) are beyond what comes to mind.

If it is asked: Are heedlessness, disbelief, aversion and the like attributed to the absence of the Lord's will for their opposites, or to His will for their occurrence?

It is said: The Qur'an has spoken of both, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those are the ones whom God did not want to purify their hearts﴾.

And He said: ﴿And whoever God wills to test, you cannot avail him anything from God﴾, and: ﴿And whoever He wills to send astray﴾.

(Section)

As for the absence of His will and desire, it is as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those are the ones whom God did not want to purify their hearts﴾.

And He said: ﴿Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾, and: ﴿Had your Lord willed, all those on earth would have believed together﴾.

The absence of His will for a thing necessitates its non-existence, just as His will necessitates its existence. What God wills must exist, and what He does not will cannot exist. He, glory be to Him, has informed that servants do not will except after His will, and do not do anything except after His will. He said: ﴿And you will not will except that God wills﴾, and: ﴿And they do not remember except that God wills﴾.

If it is asked: Can an act be within the servant's capacity while God does not will that he do it?

It is said: If by its being within capacity is meant the soundness of the servant's instruments by which he is able to act, the soundness of his limbs, the existence of his faculties, his empowerment with the causes of the act, the preparation of the way for its doing, and the opening of the path for him, then yes, it is within capacity in this sense. But if by its being within capacity is meant the capacity concomitant with the act, which necessitates it and which, once present, the act does not fail to follow, then it is not within capacity in this sense.

The clarification of this is that capacity is of two kinds. One is the capacity that makes the act valid (qudra musahhiha): the capacity of causes and conditions and the soundness of the instruments, which is the basis of moral responsibility (taklif). This precedes the act and does not necessitate it. The other is the capacity concomitant with the act, necessitating it, which the act does not fail to follow. This is not a condition of moral responsibility, so the validity and goodness of the command do not depend upon it. Thus the faith of one for whom God did not will faith, and the obedience of one for whom He did not will obedience, are within capacity in the first sense, and not within capacity in the second sense.

With this verification, the doubt concerning the imposition of what cannot be borne is removed, as its explanation will come in its proper place, God willing.

If it is asked: Did He create for one whom He knows will not believe a capacity to believe, or did He not create for him a capacity?

It is said: He created for him a capacity that makes the act valid, preceding the act, which is the basis of command and prohibition. But He did not create for him a capacity that necessitates the act and which the act does not fail to follow. That latter is His bounty, which He gives to whom He wills, and the former is His justice, by which His proof is established against His servant.

If it is asked: Can he then do the act when He has not created for him this capacity?

It is said: This is exactly the previous question, and you have known its answer. And with God is success.

[Kufr]

Kufr (disbelief) is of two kinds: greater disbelief (kufr akbar) and lesser disbelief (kufr asghar).

Greater disbelief is that which necessitates eternal abiding in the Fire.

Lesser disbelief necessitates deserving the threat (of punishment) but not eternal abiding, as in His words, exalted is He, — and it was among what was recited but whose wording was abrogated — "Do not turn away from your fathers, for it is kufr (disbelief) on your part," and the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) in a hadith: "Two things among my community are kufr (disbelief) in them: slandering lineage and wailing (for the dead)," and his saying in the Sunan: "Whoever comes to a woman in her anus has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad."

And in another hadith: "Whoever goes to a soothsayer or a fortune-teller and believes him in what he says has disbelieved in what Allah revealed to Muhammad." And his saying: "Do not return after me as disbelievers, striking one another's necks." This is the interpretation of Ibn ʿAbbas and the majority of the Companions regarding the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It is not a disbelief that removes one from the religion; rather, when one does it, it is a disbelief (of that kind), and it is not like the one who disbelieves in Allah and the Last Day." Likewise Tawus said. ʿAtaʾ said: "It is disbelief short of (full) disbelief, wrongdoing short of (full) wrongdoing, and defiance short of (full) defiance."

Among them are those who interpreted the verse as referring to abandoning judgment by what Allah has revealed while denying it; this is the view of ʿIkrimah, but it is a weaker interpretation, for the very denial of it is disbelief, whether one judges or does not judge.

Among them are those who interpreted it as referring to abandoning judgment by all that Allah has revealed; he said: this includes judging by monotheism and Islam. This is the interpretation of ʿAbd al-ʿAziz al-Kinani, and it too is far-fetched, since the threat is for negating judgment by what was sent down, and this includes suspending judgment by all of it and by part of it.

Among them are those who interpreted it as referring to judging by contradicting the text, deliberately, not out of ignorance of it nor by error in interpretation; al-Baghawi related this from the scholars in general.

Among them are those who interpreted it as referring to the People of the Book; this is the view of Qatadah, al-Dahhak and others. It is far-fetched and contrary to the apparent wording, so one should not turn to it.

Among them are those who considered it disbelief that removes one from the religion.

The correct view is that judging by other than what Allah has revealed encompasses both kinds of disbelief, lesser and greater, according to the state of the judge. If he believes it obligatory to judge by what Allah has revealed in this case, yet deviates from it out of disobedience, while acknowledging that he deserves punishment, this is lesser disbelief. If he believes it is not obligatory and that he is free to choose, while being certain that it is the ruling of Allah, this is greater disbelief. If he is ignorant of it and errs, then he is one who errs and has the ruling of those who err.

The point is that all sins are of the type of lesser disbelief, for they are the opposite of gratitude (shukr), which is acting in obedience. So a person's striving is either gratitude, or disbelief, or a third thing that is neither of these. And Allah knows best.

[Section: Greater Disbelief]

As for greater disbelief, it has five types: disbelief of denial (kufr al-takdhib), disbelief of arrogance and refusal while affirming (kufr al-istikbar wa al-ibaʾ maʿa al-tasdiq), disbelief of aversion (kufr al-iʿrad), disbelief of doubt (kufr al-shakk), and disbelief of hypocrisy (kufr al-nifaq).

As for disbelief of denial, it is the belief that the Messengers are liars. This type is rare among the disbelievers, for Allah, exalted is He, supported His Messengers and gave them of the proofs and signs of their truthfulness what established the proof with them and removed excuse, as Allah, exalted is He, said about Pharaoh and his people: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14], and He said to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, they do not deny you, but it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-Anʿam: 33].

If this is also called disbelief of denial, it is correct, since it is denial by the tongue.

As for disbelief of refusal and arrogance, it is like the disbelief of Iblis, for he did not deny the command of Allah nor oppose it with rejection; rather, he met it with refusal and arrogance. Of this type is the disbelief of one who knows the truthfulness of the Messenger and that he came with truth from Allah, but does not submit to him out of refusal and arrogance. This is the predominant form of the disbelief of the enemies of the Messengers, as Allah, exalted is He, related about Pharaoh and his people: ﴿Shall we believe in two humans like us, while their people are servants to us?﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 47].

And like the saying of the nations to their messengers: ﴿You are only humans like us﴾ [Ibrahim: 10], and His words: ﴿Thamud denied by its transgression﴾ [al-Shams: 11]. This is the disbelief of the Jews, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89], and He said: ﴿They recognize him as they recognize their own sons﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. It is also the disbelief of Abu Talib, for he affirmed him and did not doubt his truthfulness, but zealous pride took hold of him, and reverence for his forefathers, lest he turn away from their religion and testify against them with disbelief.

As for disbelief of aversion, it is that one turns away with his hearing and heart from the Messenger, neither affirming him nor denying him, neither allying with him nor opposing him, and never giving ear to what he brought at all, as one of the Banu ʿAbd Yalil said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "By Allah, I will say to you a word: if you are truthful, you are too great in my eyes for me to answer you; and if you are lying, you are too contemptible for me to speak to you."

As for disbelief of doubt, it is that one does not firmly affirm his truthfulness nor deny him, but rather doubts his matter. This doubt persists only if one compels oneself to turn away entirely from examining the signs of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), not listening to them and not paying attention to them. But if he pays attention to them and reflects upon them, no doubt remains with him, because they necessitate truthfulness, especially all together, for their indication of truthfulness is like the indication of the sun of the day.

As for disbelief of hypocrisy, it is that one displays faith with his tongue while harboring denial in his heart. This is the greater hypocrisy, and its divisions will be explained later, Allah willing, exalted is He.

[Section: Denial Is of Two Kinds: General and Specific]

Disbelief of denial (juhud) is of two kinds: general, comprehensive disbelief, and specific, restricted disbelief.

The general is that one denies the totality of what Allah has sent down and His sending of the Messenger.

The specific, restricted kind is that one denies an obligation of the obligations of Islam, or the prohibition of one of its prohibited matters, or an attribute which Allah has described Himself with, or a report which Allah has informed of, deliberately, or preferring the saying of one who opposes it over it, for some purpose.

As for denying that out of ignorance, or by an interpretation for which its holder is excused, one is not declared a disbeliever for it, like the case of the man who denied Allah's power over him and instructed his family to burn him and scatter him in the wind. Despite this, Allah forgave him and had mercy on him because of his ignorance, since what he did was the extent of his knowledge, and he did not deny Allah's power to resurrect him out of obstinacy or denial.

I translate the passage below, keeping the Qur'anic quotations in ﴿ ﴾ markers as instructed.

He informed that their return is to Him when He announced the multiplicity of their laws and methods, just as He mentioned exactly that when He announced the multiplicity of their direction and qibla. So He said: ﴿And for each there is a direction, which He faces. So race to good deeds. Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together﴾.

Beneath this lies a wonderful secret that whoever understands, understands: when there is difference in ways, creeds, laws and qiblas, the nearest of them to the truth is the one that points more clearly to Allah and conveys one to Him, because the return of all of them is to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection, however their states, times and places differ. Their return is to one Lord and one God. Thus it should be that the return of all of them, in this world, is to Him alone: they worship none other than Him and do not submit to any religion other than His, for He is their true God in this world and the next. But when most people have refused this, insisting on disbelief, and gone off on false paths, worshipping other than Him, even if they follow other religions, then you, O believers, race to good deeds and hasten toward them, and do not go with those who hasten into falsehood and disbelief. So reflect on this wonderful secret in the two surahs, the Day of Distinction and the Resurrection.

Regarding His words: ﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to differ about﴾, there is another secret as well: this difference is evidence of the Day of Distinction, the day on which Allah, exalted is He, distinguishes among the creatures and makes clear to them the reality of what they differed about. So the difference itself is evidence of the Day of Distinction and the Resurrection. The saying of the Exalted in Surat an-Nahl clarifies this: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not resurrect those who die. Yes, it is a promise binding upon Him, but most people do not know. That He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars﴾. So He, the Exalted, mentioned two far-reaching wisdoms in resurrecting the dead after causing them to die:

The first: that He may make clear to people that about which they differed. This is a visible clarification shared by all creatures, whereas the clarification that took place in this world is a faith-based clarification particular to some of them.

The second wisdom: that the falsifier may know that he was a liar, even though he was upon falsehood, and that the attribution of the people of truth to falsehood is among his fabrications, lies and slander, so that this disgraces him with the greatest disgrace. So reflect on the secrets of the speech of the Lord, exalted is He, and on the far-reaching wisdom contained in the verses of the Glorious Book, which testifies that it is the speech of the Lord of the worlds, and testifies for His Messenger that he is the truthful one, the one whose truthfulness is confirmed. All of this follows from His wisdom and praiseworthiness, exalted is He, and it is the meaning of His having created the heavens and the earth and what is between them with truth: He did not create that in vain, but created it proceeding from truth, tending toward truth, and comprising truth.

He described them with six attributes:

First: their love for Him.

Second: His love for them.

Third: their humility and gentleness towards His allies.

Fourth: their might and severity towards His enemies.

Fifth: their striving (jihad) in His cause.

Sixth: their bearing the blame of people for this, and that they are not among those whom speech and reproach turn away from striving in the cause of God. Nor are they like those who endure blame and reproach for loving what God does not love, nor like those who display before the Lord, may He be blessed and exalted, what is disliked by Him and for which they are blamed. They are called the Malamatiyya (a Sufi group who court blame), in that they openly display what they are blamed for outwardly, while inwardly they are hidden in sincerity and devotion, concealing their state from people. So these ones acted this way because they could not bear blame, whereas the first group bore blame for what God does not love, while the beloved of God did what God loves, and the blame of no blamer deterred them.

The divisions are therefore three:

First: one whom blame turns away from the objects of God's love.

Second: one whom the blame of no blamer seizes in regard to the love of God.

Third: one who displays what he is blamed for, concealing his standing in the objects of God's love.

The first is negligent, the third is a weak believer, and the middle is the middle and the best, the strong believer. The strong believer is better and more beloved to God than the weak believer. The highest thing loved by God and His Messenger is striving in the cause of God, and those who blame it are many, since most souls dislike it. Those who blame it are of three kinds: the hypocrite, the discourager who saps resolve, and the spreader of alarm who weakens strength and power.

[Section: Praiseworthy love and blameworthy love]

Since love is a genus under which there are types differing in degree and description, most of what is mentioned concerning it with respect to God, may He be exalted, is what is specific to Him and befitting of Him among its types, and what is suitable for Him alone, such as worship (ʿibadah), turning in repentance (inabah), and the like. Worship is suitable for Him alone, and so is turning in repentance. He has mentioned love by its absolute name, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So God will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him﴾.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among people are those who take, besides God, equals whom they love as they love God. But those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165].

The greatest kind of blameworthy love is love alongside God, in which the lover equates his love for God with his love for the rival he has taken besides Him.

The greatest kind of praiseworthy love is love of God alone. This love is the root and the head of happiness, the one by which no one escapes punishment except through it. Blameworthy idolatrous love is the root and the head of wretchedness, the one in which none remains in punishment except its people. So the people of love, who loved God and worshipped Him alone with no partner, do not enter the Fire, and whoever among them enters it because of his sins, none of them remains in it.

The Qur'an revolves around commanding that love and its requirements, and forbidding the other love and its requirements. It coined parables and comparisons for both kinds, related the stories of both kinds, detailed the deeds of both kinds, their allies, and the object worshipped by each of them, informed about His treatment of both kinds, and about the state of both kinds in the three abodes: the abode of this world, the abode of the barzakh (intermediate state), and the abode of permanence. The Qur'an came concerning both kinds.

The essence of the call of all the Messengers, from the first of them to the last, is only the worship of God alone, with no partner, which comprises perfect love of Him, perfect submission and humility before Him, veneration and exaltation, and the requirements of that: obedience and God-consciousness (taqwa).

It is established in the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim), from the hadith of Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, none of you believes until I am more beloved to him than his father, his child, and all of mankind."

In Sahih al-Bukhari, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of God, by God, you are more beloved to me than everything except my own self." He said: "No, O ʿUmar, until I am more beloved to you than your own self." He said: "By the One who sent you with the truth, you are more beloved to me than my own self." He said: "Now, O ʿUmar."

If this is the status of the love of His servant and Messenger (ﷺ), and the obligation of putting it before love of one's own self, one's child, one's father, and all mankind, then what is the thought about the love of the One who sent him, glorified and exalted is He, and the obligation of putting it before the love of anything else?

The love of the Lord, glorified is He, is distinct from the love of others in its degree, its quality, and in His being singled out for it. For what is obligatory for Him in all of that is that He be more beloved to the servant than his child and his father, indeed more than his hearing, his sight, and the self that is between his two sides. So his true God and the One he worships should be more beloved to him than all of that. A thing may be loved in one respect and not in another, and may be loved for something else. There is nothing loved for its own essence in every respect except God alone, and divinity is suitable for Him alone. ﴿Had there been in them gods other than God, they would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22].

And ta'alluh (devotion as to a god) is love, obedience, and submission.

(Note)

Some of the salaf (the early pious predecessors) said: "A people claimed the love of God, so God revealed the verse of the trial: ﴿Say: If you should love God, then follow me; God will love you﴾ [Al ʿImran: 31]."

And he said: "﴿God will love you﴾ [Al ʿImran: 31] points to the evidence of love, its fruit, and its benefit.

Its evidence and sign is following the Messenger.

Its benefit and fruit is the love of the Sender for you. So as long as following does not occur, your love for Him is not realized, and His love for you is absent."

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, whoever among you reverts from his religion, God will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him, humbled before the believers, mighty over the disbelievers, striving in the cause of God, and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54]. So He mentioned four signs for them. The first: that they are humble towards the believers. It was said: its meaning is that they are tender, merciful, compassionate towards them, and kind to them. Since adhillah (humble) implies this meaning, it was followed by the particle ʿala (towards). ʿAta' said: towards the believers they are like a child to his father, or a slave to his master; and towards the disbelievers they are like a lion upon its prey. ﴿Severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

The third sign: striving in the cause of God with the self, the hand, the tongue, and wealth, and this is the realization of the claim of love.

The fourth sign: that the blame of no blamer seizes them regarding God. This is the sign of the soundness of love, for every lover whom blame about his beloved seizes is not a lover in reality, as it has been said:

May whoever in you has any remnant of love for other than you never find, through it, a path to blame.

(Section)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So God will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him, humbled before the believers, mighty over the disbelievers﴾.

Since the humility from them is the humility of mercy, tenderness, compassion, and lowliness of heart, it is followed by the particle ʿala, by implicit meaning of these verbs. It does not mean the humiliation of disgrace, whose possessor is abased. Rather it is the humility of gentleness and submission, whose possessor is docile. So the believer is docile, as in the hadith: "The believer is like a docile camel."

And the hypocrite and the wicked person is abased.

And four are seized by abasement most intensely: the liar, the slanderer, the miser, and the tyrant.

His saying: ﴿mighty over the disbelievers﴾ is from the might of strength, protection, and dominance. ʿAta' (may God be pleased with him) said: towards the believers they are like a father to his child, and towards the disbelievers like a beast of prey upon its quarry, as He said in the other verse: ﴿severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. And this is the reverse of the state of those of whom it was said:

Arrogance towards us, and cowardice before your enemy. Wretched are the two traits: arrogance and cowardice.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of ʿIyad ibn Himar (may God be pleased with him), he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God revealed to me that you should be humble, so that no one boasts over another and no one oppresses another."

In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Masʿud (may God be pleased with him), he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No one who has in his heart an atom's weight of pride will enter Paradise."

In the two Sahihs, as a marfuʿ (attributed to the Prophet) report: "Shall I inform you of the people of the Fire? Every harsh, arrogant, proud person."

In the hadith of the disputation of Paradise and the Fire: "The Fire said: What is with me that only the tyrants and the arrogant enter me? And Paradise said: What is with me that only the weak of people and their rejects enter me?"

And it is in the Sahih.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Saʿid and from Abu Hurayrah (may God be pleased with them both), they both said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God, mighty and majestic, says: Might is My waist-wrapper, and greatness is My cloak. Whoever contends with Me, I will punish him."

In Jami' al-Tirmidhi, as a marfuʿ report from Salamah ibn al-Akwa' (may God be pleased with him): "A man will not cease going on with his self until he is recorded in the register of the tyrants, and there befalls him what befell them."

"The Prophet (ﷺ) used to pass by children and greet them with peace."

"A female slave would take his hand (ﷺ) and go with him wherever she wished."

"When he (ﷺ) ate, he would lick his three fingers."
