In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Usamah ibn Zayd, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and thrown into the Fire, and his entrails will spill out in the Fire, and he will go round and round as a donkey goes round its millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'O so-and-so, what is the matter with you? Did you not used to enjoin us to do good and forbid us from evil?' He will say: 'Yes, I used to enjoin you to do good but would not do it myself, and I used to forbid you from evil and would do it myself.'"

Imam Ahmad narrated from Malik ibn Dinar, who said: A scholar (hibr) of the scholars of the Children of Israel used to host men and women at his home, and he would admonish them and remind them of the Days of Allah. One day he saw some of his sons fondling the women, and he said: "Gently, my son, gently, my son." He fell from his couch, his spinal cord was severed, his wife miscarried, and his sons were killed. Then Allah revealed to their prophet: "Tell so-and-so the news: I will not bring forth from your loins a truthful person ever. Your anger was for Me only in that you said: 'Gently, my son.'"

Imam Ahmad also narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of minor sins, for they gather upon a man until they destroy him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck an example for them: they are like a people who descended into a barren land, and the people's cooking was ready. The man went out and brought a stick, and another man brought a stick, until they gathered a heap, and they kindled a fire and cooked what they had thrown into it."

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "You do deeds that seem finer in your eyes than a hair, yet in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) we used to count them among the destructive sins."

In the Sahihayn, from Abdullah ibn Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A woman was punished because of a cat she confined until it died; she entered the Fire on account of it. She neither fed it nor gave it drink when she confined it, nor did she let it eat from the creatures of the earth."

In al-Hilyah by Abu Nu'aym, from Hudhayfah, that it was said to him: "Did the Children of Israel abandon their religion in a single day?" He said: "No, but when they were commanded to do something they abandoned it, and when they were forbidden from something they engaged in it, until they stripped themselves of their religion as a man strips off his shirt."

From this, some of the salaf (early generations of Muslims) said: "Sins are the messenger of disbelief, just as kissing is the messenger of intercourse, singing is the messenger of fornication, looking is the messenger of passion, and illness is the messenger of death."

Also in al-Hilyah, from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "O one who commits a sin, do not feel secure from its evil consequence. What follows a sin is greater than the sin itself when you commit it: your little shame before those on your right and left while you are engaged in the sin is greater than the sin; your laughter while you do not know what Allah will do with you is greater than the sin; your joy at the sin when you attain it is greater than the sin; your grief over the sin when it escapes you is greater than the sin; your fear of the wind when it moves the curtain of your door while you are in sin, yet your heart does not tremble at the sight of Allah's gaze upon you, is greater than the sin. Woe to you! Do you know what Job's sin was, for which he was tested with affliction in his body and the loss of his wealth? A poor man called upon him for help against a wrongdoer whom he could have repelled from him, but he did not help him, nor did he forbid the wrongdoer from his wrongdoing, so Allah tested him."

Imam Ahmad said: al-Walid narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Awza'i say: I heard Bilal ibn Sa'd say: "Do not look at how small the sin is, but look at whom you have disobeyed."

Al-Fudayl ibn Iyad said: "In proportion as the sin seems small to you, it grows great in the sight of Allah; and in proportion as it seems great to you, it becomes small in the sight of Allah."

It has been said: Allah the Exalted revealed to Musa: "O Musa, the first of My creatures to die was Iblis, for he was the first to disobey Me, and I count among the dead only those who have disobeyed Me."

In the Musnad and Jami' al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the believer commits a sin, a black spot is made upon his heart. If he repents, gives it up, and seeks forgiveness, his heart is polished. If he increases (in sin), the spots increase until they cover his heart. That is the 'rust' (ran) of which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, spoke: ﴿Nay, but what they have been earning has covered over their hearts﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 14]."

Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a sound (sahih) hadith.

Hudhayfah said: "When a servant commits a sin, a black spot is made upon his heart, until his heart becomes like a spotted sheep."

Imam Ahmad said: Ya'qub narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Salih, from Ibn Shihab, who said: Ubayd Allah ibn Abdullah ibn Utbah narrated to me, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Amma ba'd. O assembly of Quraysh, you are fit for this authority as long as you do not disobey Allah. When you disobey Him, He will send over you one who will chastise you, just as this staff is chastised by a staff in his hand." Then he struck his staff, and it was white and hard.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Wahb, who said: The Lord, Mighty and Majestic, said, among what He says to the Children of Israel: "When I am obeyed, I am pleased; and when I am pleased, I bless; and My blessing has no end. When I am disobeyed, I become angry; and when I become angry, I curse; and My curse reaches to the seventh generation of offspring."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 5, verse 109:

﴿What is the response you were given?﴾ They say, ﴿We have no knowledge.﴾

It has been said: they said this out of courtesy toward Him, glorified is He, since they were returning the knowledge to Him.

It has also been said: its meaning is, "We have no knowledge of the reality of the inner (bātin), and only those who answered us answered outwardly (ẓāhiran). The inner is unseen, and You are the Knower of the unseen."

The verified view, God willing, is that their knowledge dissolved into His knowledge, glorified is He, and was annihilated within it, so that in comparison to Him it became as no knowledge at all. Thus they returned all knowledge to its Owner, its people, and the one most worthy of it. Their knowledge and the knowledge of all creation, in comparison with His knowledge, exalted is He, is like the drop taken by a sparrow from one of the seas of the world.

(Section)

As for the twenty-seventh question: what is the wisdom in the praise of God in the tashahhud being phrased in the third person (ghayba), even though He, glorified is He, is the One addressed whom the servant intimately addresses, while the greeting upon the Prophet ﷺ is phrased in the second person (khitab), even though he is absent?

Its answer: praise of God generally comes attached to His Most Beautiful Names, explicitly stated, not through a pronoun, unless the explicit name has been mentioned earlier, so that the pronoun follows it. This is like the worshipper's saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, Master of the Day of Recompense. You alone we worship﴾, and his saying in bowing: "Glory be to my Lord, the Mighty," and in prostration: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." Among the secret in this is that attaching praise to His Most Beautiful Names is due to what their meanings contain of attributes of perfection and sublime qualities. So he brings the explicit name, which indicates the meaning by which and for which He, exalted is He, is praised. The pronoun carries no indication of this. For this reason, when praise of Him must be addressed directly in the second person, he brings the explicit name joined with the plural mim, which indicates all the Names and Attributes, as in his saying when raising his head from bowing: "O Allah, our Lord, to You be praise." Sometimes he suffices with mentioning the Lord, exalted is He, since its wording indicates this meaning. So reflect on it, for its approach is most subtle. And consider how the supplication that contains both praise and request begins with the word "Allahumma," as in the master of seeking forgiveness: "O Allah, You are my Lord, there is no god but You. You created me and I am Your servant..." the hadith.

Narrated by al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i.

Pure supplication comes prefaced by the word "Lord," as in the saying of the believers: ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾, the saying of Adam: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾, the saying of Musa: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾, and the saying of Nuh: ﴿My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about what I have no knowledge of﴾. The Prophet ﷺ used to say between the two prostrations: "Lord, forgive me, Lord, forgive me," (sahih). The secret of this is that God is asked by His lordship, which includes His power, His beneficence, His nurturing of His servant and the rectifying of his affairs, and He is praised by His divinity, which includes affirming what is due to Him of exalted attributes and Most Beautiful Names. Reflect on the method of the Qur'an and you will find it as I have described to you. As for supplication, we have mentioned examples of it, and wherever it occurs in the Qur'an it hardly comes except prefaced by the name "Lord." As for praise, wherever it occurs it is prefaced by the Most Beautiful Names, and the greatest name with which it is prefaced is the Name of Allah, majestic is His majesty, as in: ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ wherever it comes, and like: ﴿So glory be to Allah﴾, and it came: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might﴾, and similar to it ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah﴾ wherever it occurs, and like: ﴿Blessed be Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿So blessed be Allah, the best of creators﴾, ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾, and their counterparts. And in the supplication of the Messiah came: ﴿O Allah, our Lord, send down upon us a table from the heaven﴾, so he mentioned both matters, and nothing else like it is found in the Qur'an. I have not seen anyone address this or draw attention to it. It is a wondrous secret indicating the Messiah's complete knowledge of his Lord and his veneration of Him. For this request came following his people's request of him: ﴿Is your Lord able to send down upon us a table from the heaven?﴾ So Allah admonished them and informed them that this is something unfitting to ask about, and that faith repels it. When they insisted on the request, and the Messiah feared that doubt would enter them if they were not granted what they asked, he began the request with the word ﴿Allahumma﴾, which indicates praise of Allah with all His Names and Attributes. Within this is the image of him as one who praises, who extols and mentions the Names of his Lord, praising Him through them, and that the purpose of this supplication and the fulfilling of this need is only that He be praised thereby, glorified, and that His bounties be mentioned and the signs of His power and lordship be manifested, and that it be a proof of the truthfulness of His messenger. Thereby there results an increase in faith and a praise of Allah which makes the request fitting and serves as an excuse for it. So he brought both names: the name Allah, by which He is praised, and the name Lord, by which He is called upon and asked, since the situation was one of both matters.

So reflect on this wondrous secret, and do not let your understanding stray from it, for it is among the understanding that Allah grants to whom He wills in His Book. And to Him belongs all praise.

(Question)

Allah, the Exalted, says about Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿If I had said it, You would surely have known it﴾. This is a conditional clause introduced upon a past verb, and its meaning is definitely past, because the Messiah either said this statement after he was raised to heaven, or it is a narration of what he will say on the Day of Resurrection. In both cases the condition and its response are connected to the past. Whoever says that this statement was uttered by him in the world before his raising has erred against Allah, and the intended meaning would be: "If I were to say this, You would know it." This is a distortion of the verse, because this answer was only given by him after Allah asked him about it, and Allah did not ask him while he was among his people, nor did they take him and his mother as two gods except after his raising by centuries. It is not permissible to distort the words of Allah in defense of a grammatical rule; demolishing a hundred of such rules is easier than distorting the meaning of a verse. Ibn al-Sarraj said in his Usul: "Both of them must be interpreted as two future verbs, the meaning being: if it is established in the future that I said it in the past, it will be established that You knew it. Whatever is established in the past, its establishment in the future is such that a conditional statement about it is appropriate." This answer is also very weak and the wording does not indicate it. I wonder what they make of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"If you have committed a sin, then seek forgiveness from Allah and repent to Him."

Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

Does any sensible person say that the condition here is future?

As for the first interpretation, it is definitely null here. As for the second, the artificiality of it is not hidden, and that he did not intend that it would be established in the future that you sinned in the past, so repent; nor was this meaning intended. Rather, the intended meaning is what the statement indicates: if a sin has proceeded from you in the past, then face it with repentance. Nothing else was meant by these words. When the corruption of both answers becomes clear, the correct position is to say: a conditional clause and its response is sometimes a pure hypothetical, not including an answer to a questioner ("Did such-and-such happen?") nor serving to negate the claim of one who says "such-and-such has happened." This requires the future. Sometimes it is intended and includes an answer to a questioner asking "Did such-and-such happen?" or rejects his statement "such-and-such has happened." When the response is conditioned here on a condition, it does not necessarily have to be future, neither in wording nor in meaning; rather, the future is not valid in it at all. Like one who says to a man, "Did you free your slave?" and he replies, "If I freed him, then Allah has freed him": there is no meaning of the future here at all. Likewise if you say it to someone who says, "I accompanied so-and-so," and he replies, "If I accompanied him, then I have gained good by his companionship." Likewise if you say to him, "Did you sin?" and he replies, "If I sinned, then I have repented to Allah and sought His forgiveness." Likewise if he says, "Did you say such-and-such to so-and-so?" while he knows that the other knows of his saying it to him, and he replies, "If I said it, then he knows it." You know that all these positions are positions of the past in both wording and meaning, so that the question matches the answer and the informative (khabari) conditional is valid, not the promissory (wa'di) one. The promissory conditional necessarily implies the future, whereas the informative conditional does not. Among this category is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is of the liars. And if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is of the truthful﴾. And you say: "If the witnesses testified to such-and-such, then she has spoken truly." This is a subtle point that the books of the grammarians and the scholars have not covered, and it is, as you see, clear and evident, and all praise is due to Allah.

The Lord, exalted is He, loves His own essence, His attributes, and His names. He is Pardoning (ʿAfūw) and loves pardon; He loves forgiveness (maghfirah), and He loves repentance (tawbah). He rejoices at the repentance of His servant when the servant turns back to Him with a joy greater than what can occur to the mind.

The decree of what He forgives, pardons for its doer, forbears from, accepts repentance for, and overlooks flows from the requirements of His names and attributes, and from the realization of what He loves and is pleased with of that, and of what He praises Himself for and what the people of His heavens and the people of His earth praise Him for. These are among the requirements of His perfection and the demands of His praise.

He, glorified is He, is the Praiseworthy (al-Ḥamīd), the Glorious (al-Majīd), and His praise and His glory require their effects.

Among their effects are the forgiveness of slips, the pardoning of stumbles, the pardoning of evil deeds, and the overlooking of crimes, together with His complete power to exact the right. He knows the crime and the measure of its punishment, so His forbearance comes after His knowledge, and His pardon after His power, and His forgiveness proceeds from the completeness of His might and wisdom. As the Messiah ﷺ said: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾.

That is: Your forgiveness proceeds from the completeness of Your power and wisdom. You are not like one who forgives out of weakness, or overlooks out of ignorance of the value of the right; rather You are Knowing of Your right, Able to exact it, and Wise in taking it.

Whoever reflects on the operation of the effects of the names and attributes in the world and in the command will realize that the source of the decreeing of these crimes by the servants, and their predestination, is from the perfection of the names, the attributes and the acts; and their ends too are the requirement of His praise and His glory, just as they are the requirement of His lordship and His divinity.

So in everything He decrees and predestines there is perfect wisdom, dazzling signs, and disclosures of Himself to His servants through His names and attributes, and the eliciting of their love for Him, their remembrance of Him, their gratitude to Him, and their worship of Him through His Most Beautiful Names. For each name has a specific form of worship (taʿabbud) belonging to it, in knowledge, recognition and state. The most complete of people in servitude ('ubūdiyyah) is the one who worships Him through all the names and attributes that humans can perceive, so that the servitude of one name does not veil him from the servitude of another name. Unlike one whom the worship through His name the Powerful (al-Qadīr) veils from worshipping through His name the Forbearing, the Merciful; or whose servitude to His name the Giver (al-Muʿṭī) veils him from servitude to His name the Withholder (al-Māniʿ); or whose servitude to His name the Merciful, the Pardoner, the Forgiving veils him from His name the Avenger (al-Muntaqim); or who worships through names of affection, kindness, gentleness and benevolence to the exclusion of names of justice, majesty, greatness and pride, and the like.

This is the path of the perfected among those travelling to God, a path derived from the very core of the Qur'an. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿To God belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 180]. Calling upon Him by them encompasses the supplication of request, the supplication of praise, and the supplication of worship. He, glorified is He, calls His servants to know Him by His names and attributes, to praise Him by them, and to take their share of servitude to them.

He, glorified is He, loves the requirement of His names and attributes.

So He is Knowing and loves every knower; Generous and loves every generous one; One (Witr) and loves oneness; Beautiful and loves beauty; Pardoning and loves pardon and its people; Modest and loves modesty and its people; Righteous and loves the righteous; Thankful and loves the thankful; Patient and loves the patient; Forbearing and loves the people of forbearance. Because of His love, glorified is He, for repentance, forgiveness, pardon and overlooking, He created one who forgives him, accepts his repentance and pardons him, and He predestined for him what requires the occurrence of what is disliked and hated by Him, so that what is loved and pleasing to Him may follow from it. His intermediation is like the intermediation of disliked causes that lead to what is loved.

> Often the disliked thing of the servants is the cause of what they love,
> and what is like it is a cause.

(Section)

Reflect on the states of the Messengers, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them, with God, and on their address and their questions. How do you find them all filled with courtesy and standing upon it?

The Messiah, peace be upon him, said: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 116]. He did not say: "I did not say it." There is a difference between the two answers in the reality of courtesy. Then he referred the matter to God's knowledge of the state and its secret, saying: ﴿You know what is in my soul﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 116]. Then he disavowed knowledge of his Lord's unseen and what is specific to Him, saying: ﴿And I do not know what is in Yourself﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 116]. Then he praised his Lord and described Him as singularly possessing the knowledge of all the unseen, saying: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 116]. Then he denied that he had said to them anything other than what his Lord commanded him, which is pure monotheism, saying: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship God, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 117]. Then he reported his witnessing over them for the duration of his stay among them, and that after his death he has no oversight of them, and that God, Mighty and Majestic, alone is the One who, after death, oversees them. He said: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 117]. Then he described His witnessing, glorified is He, as above and more comprehensive than every witnessing, saying: ﴿And You are Witness over all things﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 117]. Then he said: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 118]. This is among the most eloquent courtesy with God in such a station. That is: it is the way of a master to show mercy to his servants and to do good to them. These are Your servants; they are not servants of another. So if You punish them, despite their being Your servants, that is only because they are wicked servants, among the basest of servants, the most insolent toward their master and the most disobedient to Him; otherwise You would not punish them, for the closeness inherent in servitude calls for the master's kindness to his servant and his mercy.

So why would the Most Merciful of the merciful, the Most Generous of the generous, the Greatest of the doers of good punish His servants? Only because of their excessive insolence, their refusal to obey Him, and their complete deservingness of punishment.

His saying ﴿Indeed You, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 116] has already preceded; that is, they are Your servants, and You are most knowing of their secret and their open deeds. So if You punish them, You punish them with knowledge from You of what You punish them for. They are Your servants, and You are most knowing of what they committed and earned. There is in this no appeal to pity for them, as the ignorant suppose, nor a surrender to mere will and bare sovereignty devoid of wisdom, as the Qadariyyah suppose. Rather it is acknowledgment, confession, and praise of Him, glorified is He, for His wisdom, His justice, the completeness of His knowledge of their state, and their deservingness of punishment.

Then he said: ﴿And if You forgive them, indeed You, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 118], and did not say: "the Forgiving, the Merciful."

This is among the most eloquent courtesy with God, exalted is He. For he said it at a time of the Lord's anger against them and the command to send them to the Fire. So it is not a station of appeal for pity nor of intercession, but a station of disavowal of them. Had he said, "Indeed You, You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," it would have implied an appeal for pity toward His enemies against whom His anger had intensified. The station is thus one of agreement with the Lord in His anger against those upon whom the Lord is angry. So he turned away from mentioning the two attributes by which mercy, kindness and forgiveness are sought, to mentioning might and wisdom, which include the completeness of power and the completeness of knowledge.

The meaning is: if You forgive them, Your forgiveness will proceed from the completeness of power and knowledge; it is not from inability to exact vengeance on them, nor from being unaware of the measure of their crimes. This is because a servant may forgive another out of inability to take revenge on him, or out of ignorance of the measure of the wrong done to him. Perfection is the forgiveness of one who is both Able and Knowing, and He is the Mighty, the Wise. Mentioning these two attributes in this station was precisely the courtesy in address.

In some reports: the bearers of the Throne are four. Two say: "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. To You be praise for Your forbearance after Your knowledge." Two say: "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. To You be praise for Your pardon after Your power." For this reason each of these two attributes is paired with the other, as in His saying: ﴿And God is Knowing and Forbearing﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 12], and His saying: ﴿Indeed God was ever Pardoning and Competent﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 149].

(Chapter: Contentment with the decree is valid from both the believer and the disbeliever.)

Its ultimate aim is submission to God's decree and His predestination. So where is this from being content with Him as Lord, God, and the One worshipped?

Moreover, being content with Him as Lord is an obligation (fard). Indeed, it is among the most emphatic of obligations by the consensus of the Muslim community (ummah). Whoever is not content with Him as Lord, his Islam, his deeds, and his state are not valid.

As for being content with His decree, most people hold that it is recommended (mustahabb) and not obligatory. It has been said: rather, it is obligatory, and these are two opinions in the school of Ahmad (Ibn Hanbal).

So the difference between the two levels is the difference between obligation (fard) and recommendation (nadb). In the authentic divine hadith: "God, Mighty and Majestic, says: My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than the performance of what I have made obligatory upon him." This indicates that drawing near to Him, glorified is He, through performing His obligations is superior and higher than drawing near to Him through voluntary acts.

Also: being content with Him as Lord entails being content with Him and necessitates it. For being content with His lordship is the servant's contentment with what He commands him, forbids him, allots to him, decrees for him, gives him, and withholds from him. Whenever he is not content with all of that, he has not been content with Him as Lord in every respect, even if he is content with Him as Lord in some of them. So being content with Him as Lord in every respect necessitates being content with Him and includes it, without doubt.

Also: being content with Him as Lord relates to His essence, His attributes, and His names, and His general and particular lordship. It is thus being content with Him as Creator and Governor, as Commander and Forbidder, as King, as Giver and Withholder, as Judge, as Trustee and Protector, as Helper and Supporter, as Sufficient, Reckoner, and Watcher, as Tester and Healer, and as Restrainer and Expander, and so on through the other attributes of His lordship.

As for being content with Him: it is the servant's contentment with what He does to him and gives him. For this reason it has only come in relation to reward and recompense, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, pleased and pleasing [to Him]﴾ [al-Fajr: 27]. This is by her contentment with Him because of the honor that she attained from Him. As in His saying: ﴿They will abide therein forever. God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is for whoever fears his Lord﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 8].

Being content with Him is the root of being content with Him (as Lord), and being content with Him is the fruit of being content with Him as Lord.

The secret of the matter: being content with Him relates to His names and attributes, while being content with Him (as recompense) relates to His reward and recompense.

Also: the Prophet ﷺ linked tasting the sweetness of faith to whoever is content with God as Lord, and did not link it to whoever is content with Him (in the sense of being pleased with His acts). As the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever is content with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad ﷺ as Messenger, has tasted the taste of faith." Thus he made being content with Him paired with being content with His religion and His Prophet. These three are the foundations of Islam, upon which it stands and by which alone it stands.

Also: being content with Him as Lord includes His unification (tawhid) and His worship, turning back to Him (inabah), relying upon Him (tawakkul), fearing Him, hoping in Him, loving Him, and patience for Him and through Him. Gratitude for His blessings includes seeing everything from Him as a blessing and a kindness, even if His servant is displeased. Being content with Him includes the testimony that there is no god but God; being content with Muhammad as Messenger includes the testimony that Muhammad is the Messenger of God; and being content with Islam as religion includes the commitment to His servanthood and obedience to Him and to His Messenger. So these three encompass the whole religion.

Also: being content with Him as Lord includes taking Him as the one worshipped to the exclusion of all else, taking Him as protector and object of worship, and nullifying the worship of everything other than Him. God has said to His Messenger: ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than God?﴾ [al-An'am: 114], and ﴿Shall I take other than God as a protector?﴾ [al-An'am: 14], and ﴿Say: Shall I seek a lord other than God, while He is the Lord of all things?﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. This is precisely being content with Him as Lord.

Also: He made the reality of being content with Him as Lord to be that one hates the worship of what is other than Him. Whenever the servant hates the worship of anything other than God among false deities, out of love and fear, hope and veneration, and reverence, he has realized being content with Him as Lord, which is the pivot of the millstone of Islam.

It is the pivot of the millstone of religion because all beliefs, deeds, and states are founded upon the unification of God, Mighty and Majestic, in worship and the hatred of worshipping anything else. Whoever does not have this pivot does not have a millstone that turns upon it. Whoever attains this pivot has his millstone established, and it turns around that pivot. Then he exits from the circle of polytheism into the circle of Islam, and the millstone of his Islam and faith turns upon its firm, constant pivot.

Also: He made the attainment of this level of contentment dependent upon the One being content with Him as Lord, glorified is He, being more beloved to the servant than everything, the most deserving of veneration, and the most worthy of obedience. It is known that this encompasses the principles of servanthood and organizes its branches and divisions.

Since complete love is the heart's inclination with all of itself toward the beloved, that inclination necessarily leads to obedience to Him and veneration of Him. The stronger the inclination, the more complete the obedience and the more abundant the veneration. This inclination accompanies faith; indeed, it is the spirit and core of faith. What could be higher than a matter that entails that God, glorified is He, be the most beloved of things to the servant, the most deserving of veneration, and the most worthy of obedience?

By this the servant finds the sweetness of faith, as in the authentic report from him ﷺ who said: "Three qualities whoever possesses finds the sweetness of faith: that God and His Messenger be more beloved to him than anything else; that he love a person only for God's sake; and that he hate to return to disbelief after God has rescued him from it, just as he hates to be thrown into the Fire."

So he linked the tasting of faith to being content with God as Lord, and he linked the existence of its sweetness to what depends upon it and cannot be complete without it, namely that He, glorified is He, and His Messenger be the most beloved things to the servant.

Since this complete love and sincerity, whose fruit it is, are higher than mere contentment with His lordship, glorified is He, its fruit is higher: it is the finding of the sweetness of faith. The fruit of contentment is the tasting of the taste of faith. The former is finding a sweetness, the latter is tasting a flavor. And God is the One sought for help.

This and that are only consequences of being content with Him alone as Lord, of disavowing the worship of anything else, of the heart's inclination with all of itself toward Him, and of the powers of the lover all being drawn toward Him. His servant's contentment with his Lord follows from this contentment with Him. Whoever is content with God as Lord, God is content with him as a servant. Whoever is content with Him in His giving, His withholding, His trials, and His well-being, does not attain by that the rank of the Lord's contentment with him, unless he is also content with Him as Lord, with His Prophet as Messenger, and with Islam as religion. For the servant may be content with God his Lord in what He gives him and what He withholds from him, but not be content with Him alone as the One worshipped and God. For this reason, the one who is content with Him as Lord is guaranteed the servant's contentment on the Day of Resurrection, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever says each day: I am content with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as Prophet, it is a right upon God that He make him content on the Day of Resurrection."

(Section)

Having understood this, let us return to explaining his words. He said: "And with this contentment the revelation spoke."

He refers to His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿God said: This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness. For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great triumph﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119].

And He said at the end of Surah al-Mujadilah: ﴿And He will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein. God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. Those are the party of God. Unquestionably, the party of God are the successful﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22]. And at the end of Surah Lam Yakun: ﴿They will abide therein forever. God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is for whoever fears his Lord﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 8].

These verses include their reward for their truthfulness and their faith, their righteous deeds, their striving against His enemies, and their not befriending them: that God is pleased with them, so He made them content, and they were content with Him. This was attained for them only after being content with Him as Lord, with Muhammad as Prophet, and with Islam as religion.

His words: "And it is being content with Him in everything He decrees."

Here there are three matters: contentment with God, contentment with God (as Lord), and contentment with God's decree.

Being content with Him is an obligation. Being content with Him (in the sense of His acts toward the servant), though it is among the greatest matters and the noblest kinds of servanthood, has not been required of everyone, because of their weakness and the hardship it entails for them. Some scholars made it obligatory, just as they made contentment with Him as Lord obligatory, and they argued with arguments.

Among them: if he is not content with his Lord, then he is discontent with Him, since there is no intermediate state between contentment and discontent, and the servant's discontent with his Lord contradicts his being content with Him as Lord.

They said: Also, his not being content with Him entails an evil opinion of Him, disputing with Him over His choice for His servant, and that the Lord, blessed and exalted, chooses something and is pleased with it, while the servant does not choose it nor is pleased with it, and this contradicts servanthood.

They said: In some divine reports: "Whoever is not content with My decree and does not patiently endure My trial, let him take a lord other than Me."

There is no proof in any of that.

As for his saying that one cannot be freed from discontent with his Lord except by being content with Him, since there is no intermediary between contentment and discontent: this is a corrupted statement. For discontent with what is decreed does not entail discontent with the One who decreed it, just as the dislike, hatred, and aversion toward what is decreed do not entail that this attaches to the One who decreed and predestined it. The decreed thing may be disliked by the servant while he is content with the One who decreed and predestined it. Indeed, his displeasure may even coincide with contentment with the decree itself, as will come, God willing.

As for your saying that it entails the servant's ill opinion of his Lord and disputing with Him over His choice, it is not so. Rather, it is a good opinion of his Lord in both states. For he only dislikes what is decreed and disputes it with another decree, just as he disputes the decree that his Lord dislikes with the decree that He loves and is pleased with. So he disputes God's decree with God's decree, by God, toward God, just as he seeks refuge in His contentment from His anger, and in His pardon from His punishment, and seeks refuge in Him from Himself.

As for his choosing for himself what his Lord does not choose, this is a matter requiring detail, and the rule of affirmation and negation does not apply to it. The choice of the Lord, exalted is He, for His servant is of two kinds.

One: a religious, legislative choice. What is obligatory upon the servant in this category is not to choose other than what his Master has chosen for him.

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when God and His Messenger have decreed a matter, to have any choice in their affair﴾ [al-Ahzab: 36]. So the servant's choice contrary to that contradicts his faith and submission, and his contentment with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as Messenger.

The second kind: a cosmic, predestined choice, which the Lord does not dislike, such as the calamities with which God tests His servant. Fleeing from these to the decree that lifts them, repels them, and removes them does not harm him, and there is no dispute in it with lordship, though there is in it a dispute with decree by decree.

This may at times be obligatory, at times recommended, at times permissible with equal sides, at times disliked, and at times forbidden.

As for the decree that He does not love or approve, such as the decree of faults and sins, the servant is commanded to be discontent with them and forbidden to be content with them.

This is the obligatory detail regarding contentment with the decree.

(A subtle point)

Wuhayb ibn al-Ward, Sufyan al-Thawri, and Yusuf ibn Asbat gathered together.

Al-Thawri said: "Before today I used to dislike sudden death. But today I wish that I were dead."

Yusuf ibn Asbat said to him: "Why?" He said: "Because of the trial I fear."

Yusuf said: "But I do not dislike a long life."

Al-Thawri said: "Why do you dislike death?"

He said: "Perhaps I may encounter a day in which I repent and do righteous deeds."

Then it was said to Wuhayb: "What do you say?"

He said: "I do not choose anything. Whatever is more beloved to me is whatever is more beloved to God."

Then al-Thawri kissed him between his eyes and said: "A spiritual soul, by the Lord of the Ka'bah!"

This is the state of a servant for whom the condition of life and the condition of death have become equal. He stands with God's choice for him between them. Wuhayb, may Allah have mercy on him, held the lofty station of contentment (al-Rida) and other stations.
